detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is most often analyzed as a labor-market technology:
which tasks will be automated, which workers complemented, and what will happen to
wages and employment? This framing, while important, is incomplete. If AI lowers the
cost of useful cognition across work and everyday life, the central social question is not
only whether people keep their jobs but where human time, attention, and effort go when
cognitive assistance becomes cheaper. Productivity gains are not welfare gains until we
know where the saved time and effort are reallocated. This paper introduces the cognitive
windfall, the stock of time, attention, and mental effort potentially freed when AI reduces
the cost of cognition, and the human activity frontier: the full set of market and non-
market activities into which people can allocate time, from paid work and caregiving to
learning, serious leisure (Stebbins, 1992), passive consumption, and civic participation.
Drawing on Becker's theory of time allocation, task-based models of automation, and
self-determination theory, the paper identifies four regimes through which the cognitive
windfall may flow: employer and institutional capture, passive absorption, purposeful
reallocation, and capability trap. It proposes a measurement agenda anchored in time-use
surveys, AI adoption data, and platform-level usage evidence. The paper presents no
original empirical results. Its central argument is conditional: the welfare consequences of AI depend on how the cognitive windfall is allocated across the human activity frontier,
and that allocation is shaped by institutions, social capital (Putnam, 2000), autonomy,
skill, attention markets, and inequality.

title: The Workforce Operating System: A Unified Architecture for Agentic Workforce Management and Enterprise Value
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Workforce Operating System: A Unified Architecture for Agentic Workforce Management and Enterprise Value

declarations.declarationOfInterest: My work develops the Workforce Operating System — a unified architecture that prices, deploys, measures, and attributes workforce capability to enterprise value. It extends two decades of strategic human-capital measurement into the agentic-AI era, with a focus on workforce value creation in private capital.

detail.abstract: Every major operating domain in the modern enterprise has a unified system of record and control. Finance has its financial operating model, supply chain its sales-and-operations planning, sales its revenue architecture, and technology its enterprise architecture. The workforce-simultaneously the largest cost on the income statement and the largest unpulled lever of value creation on the balance sheet-has none. This paper introduces the Workforce Operating System (WOS): a unified architecture that prices, deploys, measures, and attributes workforce capacity to enterprise value with the same rigor that finance applies to capital. WOS is offered not as a new idea but as the next chapter of a measurement lineage that began with the human-capital scorecard work of the early 2000s and has matured, across two decades of strategic human-resource scholarship, to the point where the next advance is no longer analytic but architectural. The paper advances a single organizing principle-the Systems Law: artificial intelligence amplifies whatever system it inherits, chaos or value-and derives from it the sequencing requirement that an operating system must precede agentic deployment, not accompany it. It then asks why a system the field has worked toward for over twenty-five years becomes buildable only now, and locates the answer in the disciplinary seam between human-resource architecture and financial operation. Its central contribution is the attribution chain, the mechanism by which a unit of human capability is priced, deployed, measured, and traced to earnings. The paper closes by locating the natural proving ground for that mechanism in private-capital value creation, a context the literature, centered on the corporate enterprise, has not yet taken up.

detail.abstract: Traditional search-and-matching models treat the natural rate of unemployment as a structural constant, fixed by hiring frictions and by how fast idle workers lose skill. We ask what happens to that constant when retraining itself becomes cheap and AI-assisted. We build a model in which the productivity a displaced worker regains during unemployment depends not on AI access alone, but on how deeply AI is woven into daily work. The natural rate is then no longer fixed but endogenous, and its path depends on a race between automation destroying vacancies and AI improving matching and retraining. We derive the condition under which it is hump-shaped: the rate rises while automation destroys vacancies faster than matching improves, then falls once that ordering reverses. The hump is a conditional prediction, not a universal law. A central implication, the leapfrog threshold, is that a retraining worker can overtake an incumbent whose employer has adopted AI only shallowly. A panel of 298 U.S. industries from 2018 to 2026 is consistent with the displacement phase, though not a causal test that displacement is under way. The model motivates Universal Basic Cognition, publicly provided AI-literacy training, to lower the natural-rate floor and tilt the economy toward the favorable regime.

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Does recent exposure to heat blunt the effects of future shocks? I examine how runners adapt to heat stress using data on 2.6 million distance race performances. This unique setting, where runners from different home climates compete in different locations with distinct weather conditions, allows me to distinguish the impact of recent variation in climate conditions from cross-sectional differences arising from population variation or climatic sorting. I find that race performances decline steeply in day-of wet bulb temperatures above 15 C and that heat effects are smallest among runners who experienced more hot days during the three months before their race, a differential that remains even after controlling for training climate. There are diminishing returns to heat exposure in the training period, and a monthly decomposition of the training window suggests the benefits may be concentrated in the most recent weeks. These findings suggest that short-run acclimatization plays an important role in humans' capacity to adapt to heat.

title: Leadership Readiness as a Measurable Construct: An Agency-Grounded, Three-Layer Architecture for the Leadership Transition

detail.title: Leadership Readiness as a Measurable Construct: An Agency-Grounded, Three-Layer Architecture for the Leadership Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of BlackRidge Institute and developer of the Leadership Readiness Diagnostic and the Four Leadership Transitions framework. BlackRidge Systems, LLC is a commercial entity that markets and licenses these instruments. This interest is disclosed in accordance with standard academic transparency practices.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a conceptual framework and applied research synthesis. No human subject research was conducted. No institutional ethics approval was required or obtained.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All research and development costs were borne by BlackRidge Systems, LLC.

detail.abstract:
Leadership transitions are consistently treated as a promotion problem, even though the empirical patterns that follow senior appointments often implicate more than the individual leader's current competence (Conger & Nadler, 2004; Berns & Klarner, 2017). Successor outcomes can be shaped by predecessor effects, the succession process itself, and a mismatch between the successor's narrow expertise and the broader contextual demands of the new role, indicating that transition outcomes can fail for reasons that are not reducible to present-role performance alone (Conger & Nadler, 2004). This working paper stipulates leadership readiness as the state of being prepared to perform effectively in a leadership role one does not yet occupy, and argues that readiness should be modeled as a target-and context-sensitive state rather than treated as an intuitive label for competence proxies (Conger & Nadler, 2004; Gabarro, 1987). 
The construct is organized using a social-cognitive agency macro-frame connected to Bandura's social cognitive tradition as it has been explicitly applied to leadership functioning through leadership self-efficacy (McCormick, 2001). The paper specifies a three-layer architecture: a Vertical Capacity Core justified by evidence that developmental architecture predicts multi-source leadership effectiveness ratings; Transition-Specific Readiness mapped to discrete passages (SHIFT, ARENA, ASCENT, EDGE), consistent with evidence that role transitions trigger identity work, anxiety, threat, and non-default lingering identities that persist beyond role change; and Context and Trajectory, grounded in research showing that leadership changes are organizational turning points with identifiable predictors and consequences beyond the focal individual (Bartone et al., 2007; Harris & Kuhnert, 2008; Wittman, 2019; Yip et al., 2019; Berns & Klarner, 2017).
This architecture is positioned as an extension of developmental readiness work that distinguishes motivational and ability components of readiness-to-develop, specifying a downstream performance criterion, adding a transition-specific middle layer, and adding an explicit contextual and trajectory layer (Avolio & Hannah, 2009; Hannah & Avolio, 2010). The construct is falsifiable: it is wrong if readiness measures fail incremental validity over established baselines, collapse onto developmental-readiness factors, or if the proposed layers do not empirically separate (Harris & Kuhnert, 2008; Hannah & Avolio, 2010).

title: Talent Feeders and U.S. AI Innovation Capacity: A Three-Clock Sequencing Framework for High-Skilled Immigration, Domestic STEM Production, and Federal R&D

detail.title: Talent Feeders and U.S. AI Innovation Capacity: A Three-Clock Sequencing Framework for High-Skilled Immigration, Domestic STEM Production, and Federal R&D

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available aggregate data and did not involve human participants; ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: U.S. artificial-intelligence competitiveness depends on a full industrial stack that includes compute, hardware, energy, data infrastructure, logistics, procurement, and security policy. This paper focuses on one critical layer of that stack: the intangible talent-and-knowledge capital system that supports AI innovation capacity. The focus is grounded in endogenous-growth and knowledge-production theories, which treat human capital, research effort, and idea production as central inputs to innovation rather than as background conditions. Within this layer, high-skilled immigration can affect firms quickly through H-1B access, transfers, extensions, and administrative friction; domestic science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) production expands more slowly through a multi-year education pipeline; and federal-funded research and development (R&D) shifts through public budget cycles. The paper develops a three-clock sequencing framework and an empirically calibrated dynamic policy-simulation model to evaluate how these channels shape U.S. AI innovation capacity. Using real Business R&D as the private-sector innovation-capacity outcome and U.S. AI patents as an AI-output bridge, the analysis calibrates feeder-growth relationships over a 2007–2024 core window, validates the model through historical reproduction, and projects alternative feeder-policy scenarios to 2035 with Monte Carlo uncertainty bands. The results show positive calibrated relationships for H-1B approvals, lagged domestic STEM bachelor’s completions, and federal-funded R&D, with robustness across alternative H-1B measures, macroeconomic controls, and an extended 2000–2024 window. The central finding is a timing mismatch: weakening a fast feeder such as high-skilled immigration creates a near-term innovation-capacity gap that slower domestic STEM expansion may eventually close but cannot prevent. In the restrictive continuation scenario, deterministic projections place 2035 Business R&D 6.8 percent below baseline. The policy implication is that, within the talent-and-knowledge capital layer of AI competitiveness, leadership depends less on choosing between immigration, domestic STEM, and R&D than on sequencing fast and slow feeders together.

detail.abstract:
The sales landscape has dramatically transformed in the last 20 years. Many of these changes were unanticipated by either sales practitioners or sales scholars at the time of the 2005 special issue on Advancing the Field of Selling and Sales Management, published in the Journal of Personal Selling & Sales Management. importantly, these shifts in complex selling environments are drastically transforming contemporary selling approaches, sales organization structures, and salesperson roles, raising numerous novel questions and challenges for sales management in the domains of motivation, control, and compensation & incentive (MCCI) systems. therefore, this paper aims to update the observations on Mcci research presented by Brown, evans, Mantrala, challagalla (2005) in the 2005 special issue, to document and stimulate further advances in sales research and practice in these domains. specifically, this study pursues the following three objectives: (i) Review the progress in research over the last two decades on MCCI systems issues raised by Brown et al.; (ii) review academic and practitioner literatures on new questions about MCCI systems arising from disruptive shifts in today's evolving selling environment, and (iii) propose an updated agenda and directions for future integrative and cross-disciplinary theoretical and empirical research on MCCI systems. 

The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1080/08853134.2025.2612491

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence markets are structurally oriented toward labor substitution rather than human capability expansion. This paper proposes a policy architecture to redirect AI development and deployment: an AI Complementarity Test of six operational criteria, and seven policy instruments spanning procurement, taxation, training, innovation funding, worker voice, and development finance. Building on Acemoglu, Autor, and Johnson (2026), this paper contributes the implementation architecture that converts principles into actionable policy levers. Instruments are sequenced from near term procurement reforms to longer term institutional restructuring, with adaptations for different state capacity contexts. The compact is further positioned in relation to existing frameworks, the EU AI Act, the U.S. NIST AI RMF, and ILO governance instruments, showing where it complements rather than duplicates current regulatory efforts. The paper addresses a gap between diagnostic frameworks and operational instruments, proposing a structured, scorable test for classifying AI deployments as worker complementary or automation biased at the use case level.

title:

A Literature Review and Critical Research Agenda
affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology,  and KTH Royal Institute of Technology

detail.title:
Implementing Artificial Intelligence Empowered Financial Advisory Services:
A Literature Review and Critical Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Robo-advisors, also known as robo-advisory services, significantly reshape customer service in financial advisory industries, transforming retail investor markets by substituting human financial advisory experts with artificial intelligence empowered services. However, existing literature remains scattered across disciplines, with theories on financial customer service predominantly focused on Internet banking, neglecting artificial intelligence empowered interactions. Thus, service providers need a framework for implementing robo-advisors in frontline service and researchers require an advanced agenda to stimulate future research. Through a systematic, interdisciplinary literature review based on Belanche et al.'s service robot framework, this article contextualizes service robot theories into financial advisory services, synthesizing knowledge on artificial intelligence empowered customer service. We contribute to literature on service robots by contextualizing, refining, and extending the original framework by Belanche et al. and by developing a research agenda with critical perspectives. Moreover, the study yields practical and theoretical insights into artificial intelligence empowered financial advisory services.

title: Friends or Rivals? Elite Peers and Upward Mobility of Non-Elites in Colonial India

detail.title: Friends or Rivals? Elite Peers and Upward Mobility of Non-Elites in Colonial India
detail.abstract: How does exposure to elite peers affect the upward mobility of non-elites in a socially stratified society? Using novel data on high school and university graduates in colonial India between 1894 and 1921, I examine how exposure to elite (upper-caste) peers in high schools affected the likelihood that nonelites progressed through university or entered the legal profession as lower-grade lawyers (mukhtars). Exploiting the plausibly random variation in the share of elite peers across cohorts within the same school, I find that a greater exposure to elite peers reduced the probability that non-elites-particularly merchant-caste students-completed university or appeared for the mukhtarship examination. These effects are driven by elites whose traditional status was linked to white-collar occupations, rather than by landowning elites. Taken together, these results imply that status-preserving elites function as rivals rather than supportive peers to non-elites in competitive educational environments.

title: Text and Voice-augmented AI Chatbots: The Role of Input Modality in Conversational Commerce
affiliations: University of California Irvine, University of California, Davis and University of Washington

detail.title: Text and Voice-augmented AI Chatbots: The Role of Input Modality in Conversational Commerce
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have become increasingly prevalent on e-commerce platforms, enabling users to interact with firms through conversational interfaces rather than traditional menu-based search. More recently, platforms have augmented text-based chatbots with voice input capabilities. Using data from a large mobile commerce platform, we examine the effects of chatbot use and voice augmentation on user engagement. Our results show that both text-only and voice-augmented chatbot interactions increase click activity and purchase outcomes, and reduce revisit time relative to manual search. However, the incremental benefits of voice augmentation over text-only interactions are not significant for the purchase-to-click ratio, suggesting that voice primarily increases purchases through greater exploration rather than higher conversion efficiency. Moreover, while voice augmentation generates larger increases in click activity for high-complexity, attribute-intensive tasks (e.g., travel and entertainment), its benefits for purchase outcomes are weaker in these settings. Finally, the benefits of voice augmentation diminish as users gain tenure on the platform. These findings contribute to research on conversational commerce and voice-enabled conversational agents by identifying important boundary conditions of voice augmentation and highlighting the role of voice-related cognitive costs in shaping user engagement.

title: AI Exposure Measures Are Not Interchangeable: Evidence from U.S. Business Dynamics, 2018-2026

detail.title: AI Exposure Measures Are Not Interchangeable: Evidence from U.S. Business Dynamics, 2018-2026
detail.abstract: I show that the most-used indices of AI exposure do not agree on what exposure means and that they can detect different channels of disruption in applied settings. A capabilitybased family is near-collinear at the industry level, a machine-learning-suitability measure is partially related to it, and a patent-overlap measure is essentially orthogonal to all three. I test the measures against realized Claude use and two U.S. business-dynamics datasets (BFS new-business applications and BED gross job flows). New-business formation does not yet respond differentially to any of the ex-ante exposure indices at the industry level. However, capability-based AI exposure is associated with elevated industrylevel gross job losses post-o3-and the realized-use automation share runs in the opposite direction from ex-ante capability on the same panel, so potential and realized AI use do not map to business dynamics the same way.

title: The Economics of Digital Addiction in Attention Markets

detail.title: The Economics of Digital Addiction in Attention Markets
detail.abstract: I first present an economic model of digital addiction in attention markets that is easily interpretable for policymakers, attorneys, and academics without an economics background. The model reveals a connection between product addictiveness and the incentives introduced by digital advertising business models. Second, I aggregate relevant findings from psychology, neuroscience, and technology studies to substantiate the assumptions that underlie the economic model. This permits the model's conclusions to move beyond the realm of incentives to the domain of real-world causation: if a firm chooses to monetize a digital product through advertising, and all else is equal, we should expect the product to become more addictive than if it were otherwise monetized (e.g., through subscription pricing). Third, I present policy solutions to reduce digital addiction, whether by removing the incentive to addict users or restricting the mechanisms whereby firms do so.

title: Competition and Consumer Search in the Shadow of Collusion
affiliations: Boston College and Brandeis University

detail.title: Competition and Consumer Search in the Shadow of Collusion
detail.abstract: Even when collusion does not arise, its mere possibility can raise prices, providing additional motivation for strong antitrust enforcement. We extend canonical sequential search models by introducing a probability of being in a "collusive state" in which firms price at monopolistic levels and characterize possible equilibria. Consumers learn about the state and the returns to search from observed prices. In all equilibria, unless search costs are prohibitively high, firms charge the monopoly price with positive probability in the "competitive state." We characterize the unique equilibrium when the prior probability of collusion is small. We find that average equilibrium transaction prices and search costs in the competitive state increase following the introduction of a small possibility of collusion.

title: Privacy-Preserving Credit Risk Prediction with Alternative Data
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics, , University of Delaware - Accounting & MIS and Lerner College of Business and Economics, University of Delaware

detail.title: Privacy-Preserving Credit Risk Prediction with Alternative Data
detail.abstract: Credit risk prediction, or how to develop predictive models that aid financial institutions in granting and managing consumer credit, is a critical problem in the consumer credit industry. Traditionally, financial institutions construct credit risk prediction models using borrowers' demographic, financial, and credit history data, collectively referred to as traditional data. Recent studies have demonstrated that alternative data, such as borrowers' mobile phone communication data, enable lenders to acquire fuller and more accurate profiles of borrowers' creditworthiness, thereby improving credit risk prediction performance. Nevertheless, alternative data are held by external entities independent of financial institutions. Directly sharing alternative data with financial institutions infringes on consumer privacy, yet existing credit risk prediction studies largely overlook this issue. To address this research gap, we define a new problem, namely privacy-preserving credit risk prediction with alternative data, which simultaneously considers three practical constraints for building credit risk prediction models with alternative data: the privacy-preserving constraint that protects consumer privacy, the model-confidentiality constraint that learns and stores the model centrally at the financial institution, and the lossless constraint that maintains the performance of the learned model. To solve this problem, we develop PrivacyCredit, a novel privacy-preserving machine learning method. We then theoretically demonstrate the privacy-preserving, model-confidential, and lossless properties of Priva-cyCredit. Through extensive experiments using a real-world credit dataset linked with alternative data, we demonstrate the predictive value of securely incorporating alternative data into credit risk prediction and show that PrivacyCredit achieves the same predictive performance as the model learned from the insecure plaintext combination of traditional and alternative data. We further evaluate its model-confidentiality property and computational efficiency, showing that PrivacyCredit can be practically implemented for credit risk prediction.

title: The CFA Franc and the Mechanics of Monetary Servitude in Francophone Africa

detail.title: The CFA Franc and the Mechanics of Monetary Servitude in Francophone Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This paper was undertaken independently as a personal research project motivated by an academic interest in monetary sovereignty, development, and political economy.

detail.abstract: Created by decree in 1945, the CFA franc remains the legal tender of fourteen African states more than six decades after their formal independence. Its defenders, concentrated in European financial institutions and among a stratum of African leadership, argue that the arrangement delivers monetary stability and low inflation by anchoring member economies to a credible external currency. A substantial body of scholarship in political economy contends, by contrast, that the system functions as an instrument of neocolonial extraction. This paper examines the structural mechanics of the franc zone-the fixed parity, the guaranteed convertibility, the historic centralisation of foreign reserves in the French Treasury, and France's voting presence on the issuing central banks-and assesses their consequences for monetary sovereignty, industrialisation, and domestic credit. It argues that the system's design privileges nominal stability and the free repatriation of capital over the developmental autonomy of its members, and that the celebrated stability is real but appears to have come at the cost of growth and structural transformation. The paper concludes by evaluating the proposed transition to the "Eco" currency, arguing that, on the evidence available in 2026, the reform alters the symbolism of the arrangement more than its underlying logic. This essay does not attempt a causal identification of the franc zone's developmental effects; it offers a structural and institutional analysis, distinguishing where the evidence is suggestive from where it is conclusive.

detail.abstract: This study examines dynamic beta estimation within a linear Gaussian state-space framework, focusing on how differences in information sets affect estimation outcomes. We begin by explicitly defining the predicting, filtering, and smoothing information sets and reconstruct the state-space model based on these definitions. This allows us to present a unified framework in which the Kalman filter, the EM algorithm, and ordinary least squares can be interpreted consistently from the perspective of information sets. Furthermore, the study introduces an integrated approach to variance estimation. Unlike conventional methods that either fix the variances or optimize the observation and state error variances independently, our framework jointly estimates both variances in a coherent manner. This approach enhances the consistency and comparability of dynamic beta estimates. In addition, we examine the testability of error-structure assumptions and conduct an empirical analysis using TOPIX and the Nikkei 225 to evaluate how index selection influences dynamic beta estimation. Because the study reorganizes the foundational theory of state-space models, the references are intentionally limited to standard sources. AI Disclosure Statement: AI tools were used only for English translation and language refinement. All research design, analysis, mathematical derivations, and substantive writing were conducted by the author.

title: Stocking Outer Space: A Compliance Market for Recycling Space Debris

detail.title: Stocking Outer Space: A Compliance Market for Recycling Space Debris

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Memphis Law Review, forthcoming Spring 2027

detail.abstract:
In recent years, regulators in major spacefaring nations have converged on one answer to orbital congestion: deorbit defunct satellites quickly and let them burn in the atmosphere. This Article calls this response the “Burn Consensus” and argues that, although it began with good intentions, it has become an expensive mistake. As the commercial space era and mega-constellations push the satellite population significantly higher, atmospheric incineration has quietly become a routine mode of industrial disposal; one that needlessly destroys valuable orbital material and could erode the ozone layer. Thus, a rule meant to reduce collision risk now wastes orbital capital and imposes atmospheric costs that existing debris policy was never built to price.

But the obstacle to a recycling alternative is not technological but legal. The Outer Space Treaty’s perpetual jurisdiction, the Liability Convention’s immovable liability, and the failure of the salvage analogy together make space derelicts something no one may lawfully touch and liabilities that no one may lawfully assume. Grounding its design in existing space law, this Article launches the missing regulatory framework for recycling through three components: (a) a Declaration of Availability, by which owners, with their supervising State’s consent, can signal a derelict’s availability for transfer; (b) Functional Liability Substitution, which leaves sovereign liability intact while shifting its practical financial burden onto recyclers; and (c) a Materials Stockyard, where transfer for reuse counts as compliant disposal. Together, these components can jumpstart a circular space economy in which congested orbits are cleared without reducing valuable orbital mass to ash.

title:
Interest Rates Without an Anchor: Multi-Window Percentiles, Exhaustive Testing, and the Pricing Logic of the China-U.S. Yield Spread
—On the Dual-Anchor Regime and Institutional Interface Theory of Global Asset Pricing
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Interest Rates Without an Anchor: Multi-Window Percentiles, Exhaustive Testing, and the Pricing Logic of the China-U.S. Yield Spread
—On the Dual-Anchor Regime and Institutional Interface Theory of Global Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: How to determine whether a sovereign bond is “fairly valued” remains an unresolved question in fixed income research. Traditional term structure models focus on the dynamics of yields but do not address where current yields stand in their own history. This paper proposes a valuation framework for sovereign bonds based on multi-window historical percentiles. The core indicator is the “price percentile” (1 – yield percentile), complemented by the “numerical percentile” of interest rate spreads, forming a two-dimensional valuation system. Exhaustive strategy backtests are conducted on three Chinese government bond ETFs (6,660 combinations) and four U.S. Treasury ETFs (186,000 combinations) using real ETF total return data. This paper proposes and verifies three theoretically innovative core propositions: (1) The “regime wandering” hypothesis of interest rates—interest rates do not possess a stable “equilibrium value” but rather “wander” within wide bands determined by monetary policy regimes. The “fair” valuation zone is rare and transitory across all four major economies examined (China, the U.S., Germany, and Japan); Japan spends over half of its time in the “extremely expensive” state, and Germany’s longest streak lasted 13.5 years. This finding directly challenges the equilibrium rate theory represented by the natural rate hypothesis of Wicksell and the Taylor Rule. (2) The hierarchical structure of institutional interfaces—the launch of Shanghai crude oil futures (SC) “activated” the previously silent pricing function of the China-U.S. yield spread in crude oil (the coefficient changed from insignificant to significant with the correct sign), while the introduction of the Shanghai Gold Benchmark Price (SGE) “enhanced” the stability of the previously sign-unstable physical-demand pricing channel in gold (nested F = 750.27), demonstrating that institutional interfaces can be classified into “activation type” and “enhancement type.” (3) The “Dual-Anchor Regime” theory of global asset pricing—the China-U.S. yield spread is the systematic variable driving the valuation divergence between the two countries’ interest rates (in-sample R² = 0.315; pseudo out-of-sample predictive correlation = 0.963); the sign of the spread serves as the critical threshold for regime switching, and Chinese macro-financial variables acquire independent marginal pricing power under the inverted-spread regime. The exhaustive backtesting results show that valuation percentile signals can systematically improve the risk-return profile of medium- and long-term government bond portfolios, with the optimal strategy paradigm being “extreme reversal + trend filter,” and the full-history window achieves the highest or near-highest Sharpe ratios in both markets; the strict monotonicity between window length and Sharpe ratio rules out overfitting. The lower number of strategy combinations for China (6,660) relative to the U.S. (186,000) arises because Chinese bond ETFs were in a prolonged one-sided rally during the sample period—simple strategies already produced high Sharpe ratios, and the exhaustive testing focused on verifying cross-duration robustness. The U.S. market, having experienced multiple rate cycles and extreme volatility, required finer exhaustive testing on parameters such as volatility filters and position scaling. This difference itself reflects the framework’s adaptability to distinct market regimes. This paper shares the same factor-screening and verification philosophy as Tang (2026)’s dual-anchor commodity pricing model—both employ exhaustive testing to let data automatically select the optimal factor combinations, and both enforce strict statistical constraints to ensure robustness. Tang (2026) discovered on the commodity side that the China-U.S. yield spread is a cross-market pricing factor; this paper reveals on the interest rate side the transmission mechanism of this factor—the China-U.S. yield spread drives the valuation divergence of the two countries’ government bonds, which in turn affects global capital allocation and commodity pricing. This paper challenges or complements several classical theories: it provides new empirical evidence and theoretical boundary conditions for equilibrium rate theory (the “fair” zone is rare, and interest rates do not fluctuate around an equilibrium), factor pricing models (factor weights switch with the macro regime), international monetary system theory (the institutional infrastructure conditions for pricing power), and behavioral finance (the asset-specificity of valuation momentum enhancement).

detail.title: Same Risk, Different Price: Dealer Rents in Single-Stock Leveraged ETFs
detail.abstract: Over-the-counter markets rarely reveal the price at which dealers bear risk. Single-stock leveraged ETFs are an exception: a registered fund must disclose the financing terms of the total-return swap that delivers its leverage, so hand-collecting these disclosures across the universe lets us observe the price of concentrated single-name risk directly, not infer it from returns. This price averages ten times the disclosed fee and six and a half times that of a matched broad-index fund, and it prices the firm-specific risk a dealer cannot diversify: volatile but diversified sector funds are financed like the broad index, while only single names command a premium. Yet the same risk does not carry one price: in a given quarter, different dealers finance identical exposure at materially different rates, inconsistent with a single law-of-one-price benchmark. Swap terms do not explain the gap, and it widens with the quantity a dealer warehouses, the signature of a rent on scarce intermediary capacity. The findings suggest that counterparty-level disclosure can make visible a rent that ordinary fee disclosures miss.

detail.title: Identifying influential spreaders in cryptocurrency networks: An effective-distance gravity strength centrality method
detail.abstract: Identifying influential spreaders is critical for analyzing contagion dynamics in complex networks. This paper proposes an effective-distance gravity strength centrality (EGSC) method to identify crucial influential spreaders in cryptocurrency networks, which integrates node strength, effective distance, and gravity model to capture both static topological features and dynamic asymmetric interactions between nodes. We adopt the Susceptible-Infected (SI) model, imprecision function, and Kendall coefficient to test the effectiveness of our method.  Empirical results on 39 cryptocurrencies from 2018 to 2024 show that EGSC outperforms degree centrality, gravity centrality, and effective-distance gravity centrality in node discrimination and ranking accuracy.  The cryptocurrency network exhibits a hierarchical hub structure.  Ethereum has the widest diffusion scope, while Bitcoin possesses the strongest spreading influence. External shocks such as the pandemic and regulatory events enhance network connectivity and strengthen global contagion. The proposed EGSC provides a general framework for identifying influential spreaders in directed and weighted financial networks, which can be extended to other complex network systems.

title: Unwritten Rules: Supervisory Discretion during the Great Depression
affiliations: and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Unwritten Rules: Supervisory Discretion during the Great Depression
detail.abstract: Does examiner human capital matter for bank supervision? Using newly digitized examination reports from the 1920s, we study a supervisory framework in which examiners flagged banks for persistent interbank borrowing that statutory limits did not address. Banks under supervisory concern were twice as likely to fail during the Great Depression, and this predictive content was largely soft information unexplained by observable balance sheet data. Banks that reduced their borrowing still failed, indicating that examiners identified a symptom of fragility rather than its source. Examiner judgment can therefore strengthen supervision, but only when supported by institutions that make discretion reliable.

detail.title: Hearing and Seeing the Fed: Multimodal Signals Beyond Text in Intraday Option Markets
detail.abstract: We study how equity and option markets process the full multimodal content of FOMC press conferences. We combine 30-second SPY, SPY-option, and SPX/SPXW-option data with video recordings of 60 Powell-era press conferences and extract synchronized textual, acoustic, and facial-expression signals. Quoted spreads and at-the-money implied volatility rise around the policy statement and compress during the Q&A, with the strongest implied-volatility declines in short-maturity options. Option demand also rotates away from 0DTE contracts as the Q&A resolves same-day policy-event risk. Conditional on text, market controls, and FOMC-day fixed effects, audio and video features predict subsequent option volume, implied volatility, and skew. Group-structured regularization and XGBoost further show that multimodal signals forecast intraday SPY returns out of sample and generate average per-trade returns of up to 15.6 percentage points in 0DTE options net of the full bid-ask spread.

detail.abstract: The aim of the study is to investigate the effect of the interaction of migration background and gender on COVID-19 vaccination intentions. We formulate a model where COVID-19 vaccination intention is a function of fears of infection, political trust, health consciousness, religiosity and the interaction of migration background and gender. We use third party online access panel data (n=1009) collected between March 15 and March 25, 2021. Qutoas were set for age and gender groups according to the distribution of the online population in Germany. First generation migrants were oversampled and resulted in a 50% share of first generation migrants and a 50% share of respondents without any migration background. title: Self-preferencing: the Zelig of competition policy in digital markets
affiliations: Università degli Studi della Basilicata and International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE)

detail.title: Self-preferencing: the Zelig of competition policy in digital markets
detail.abstract: Self-preferencing is often described as a ubiquitous feature of digital markets. The emergence of AI services is expected to further intensify attention and concerns regarding the strategies that large online platforms may adopt to grant preferential treatment to their own products and services. As a result, policymakers and competition authorities worldwide have embarked on a hunt for this perceived new menace, launching an ever-growing array of regulatory measures and antitrust probes. Yet, at this stage, no one has been able to draw a clear profile of the wanted, as a wide range of distinct practices seem to fit the description. Like a perfect Zelig, self-preferencing appears everywhere because it resembles everything. Against this background, the paper argues that the significance of self-preferencing has been largely overstated. First, selfpreferencing does not exist as a distinct legal or economic concept: it is merely a catch-all label describing a mild form of vertical integration that encompasses a variety of practices already addressed under existing competition law provisions. Second, the notion is far from novel as similar conduct and strategies have long been standard practice among traditional brick-andmortar retailers. Finally, the economic literature provides evidence that such practices are not necessarily detrimental to consumer welfare, suggesting that blanket prohibitions would be unjustified.

detail.abstract:
Executive Summary

Illinois has earned national recognition for reforms related to juvenile records and to K-12 discipline, yet a critical policy gap remains: the "collateral consequences" of school disciplinary records. Often documenting minor infractions, these records create enduring barriers to higher education and professional licensure—functioning as permanent punishment for childhood and adolescent behavior from a period of cognitive development. This Spotlight examines how disciplinary records impede Illinois students' post-graduation opportunities and proposes strategies to prevent past mistakes from becoming lifelong obstacles.

Barriers to Access: Analysis of Disciplinary Records in Admissions

The impact of school discipline extends far beyond K-12 classrooms. Despite no evidence linking past discipline to campus safety, nearly 40% of Illinois colleges using the Common Application—used by more than a thousand colleges and universities nationally—still require disclosure of these records (based on the author's analysis of 2023 application requirements). This creates a systemic barrier: 89% of institutions that collect this data use it in admissions decisions, with 29% automatically denying admission for certain offenses (Weissman & NaPier, 2015).

Beyond direct denial, these inquiries create a "chilling effect," discouraging qualified candidates from completing applications because of the burden of self-disclosure. This barrier extends into professional life: applications for law, dentistry, and physical therapy graduate programs—and the Illinois Bar itself—require disclosure of school misconduct, at times even including records from before high school. By allowing these records to persist, the state permits adolescent infractions to jeopardize professional careers decades later.

The Equity Imperative: Disproportionality and Social Justice

The reliance on disciplinary records poses a serious equity concern. As shown in Figure 1, Illinois schools that ask about disciplinary history tend to have lower levels of racial and socioeconomic diversity. By using these records to screen applicants, institutions risk importing the well-documented racial biases of K-12 discipline systems into their admissions processes.

When institutions use these records to gatekeep admission, they inadvertently import the systemic biases of the K-12 system. Data from the Illinois State Board of Education reveals that Black students represent 42.3% of out-of-school suspensions despite making up only 16.5% of the total student population. Students with disabilities who qualify for Individualized Education Plans represent 28.6% of suspensions while making up only 16% of enrollment. Amplifying the impact of these exclusionary policies through the use of disciplinary history questions risks disproportionately harming the very populations the state is working to support.

Implications for Policy

The primary justification for maintaining these records is often cited as campus safety. However, empirical data contradict this premise. Studies comparing campuses that "ban the box" regarding school discipline with those that do not have found no significant difference in crime rates (Olszewska, 2007). Moreover, from a developmental perspective, childhood prognoses are a poor predictor of adult conduct (Sampson & Laub, 2003). Research into brain maturation suggests that teenagers are prone to impulsive behavior that they naturally outgrow as they age (Piquero, 2008).

Furthermore, while institutions sometimes fear that failing to vet applicants' records will lead to legal liability, maintaining these inquiries may actually expose institutions to additional legal risk. Addressing this issue requires a legislative framework that protects institutions while prioritizing student rehabilitation and the reality of adolescent brain development.

Strategic Recommendations: A Framework for Reform

To dismantle these barriers, Illinois should address both how discipline records are maintained and how records are used. The following actions are recommended to ensure a fair path for all Illinois residents:

· Implement "Ban the Box" for School Discipline Records: Prohibit postsecondary institutions and licensing boards from inquiring about K-12 disciplinary history on initial applications.

· Establish Robust Expungement Protocols: Authorize automatic expungement of school records after a set period or upon graduation, mirroring juvenile justice models in Illinois to provide students a "clean slate."

detail.abstract:
Executive Summary

Community water fluoridation has been a cornerstone of U.S. public health for over 75 years and is recognized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as one of the ten greatest public health achievements of the 20th century (Koppaka, 2011). Illinois, which has mandated fluoridation since 1967, ranks fourth nationally with over 98% of residents receiving fluoridated water (CDC, 2022). However, scrutiny has intensified. A 2024 federal court labeled current fluoride exposure an “unreasonable risk” (Food & Water Watch, Inc. v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2024). In 2025, 21 states introduced anti-fluoridation bills, and Illinois HB 4321 would allow local opt-outs (Illinois General Assembly, 2025). This brief examines the potential consequences of removing community water fluoridation for policymakers, public health agencies, health care systems, and residents, with particular focus on Illinois populations at elevated risk for dental caries (i.e., cavities).

What does the evidence show?

Extensive evidence shows that community water fluoridation reduces dental caries in children and adults, even with widespread fluoride toothpaste use, and is highly cost-effective—each dollar invested yields $32 in avoided dental costs, with projected national savings of $6.7 billion (O'Connell et al., 2016). Oral disease also imposes substantial societal costs, including roughly 51 million lost school hours and 92 million lost work hours annually; more than 100 health organizations endorse fluoridation as an effective population-level intervention (Koppaka, 2011).

At the same time, a 2024 National Toxicology Program (NTP) report concluded that higher fluoride exposures—typically above 1.5 mg/L—are associated with lower IQ in children, though evidence at standard U.S. fluoridation levels (0.7 mg/L) remains mixed. The National Academies found that neurodevelopmental effects at community water levels are not convincingly demonstrated, underscoring uncertainty around dose and cumulative exposure. These uncertainties, combined with the 2024 federal court ruling, have heightened public concern and spurred legislative action nationwide.

What’s next?

The risks and benefits of community water fluoridation continue to be evaluated. Strong evidence supports its oral health and cost benefits, but these must be weighed against emerging neurodevelopmental concerns, rising bottled water use, and political pressures. In Illinois, HB 4321 and media coverage signal growing public and legislative scrutiny. Regardless of policy direction, the key question is whether decision-makers will plan for downstream impacts and invest in capacity, workforce, and reimbursement to meet rising demand—especially for Medicaid-enrolled children and rural communities relying on already stretched safety-net providers.

detail.abstract: Internal organization gives managers discretion to allocate hiring across units and locations. We study whether managers use the geography of new hiring as an internal allocation margin to manage prospective workforce-adjustment risk associated with future separation costs. Because unemployment insurance (UI) tax schedules are experience rated and rise with firms’ layoff histories, multi-state firms face differing expected separation costs across states. Using Lightcast job postings matched to state UI tax rules from 2010–2024, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in UI tax exposure is associated with about five fewer postings at the median firm–state–year, with little evidence of lower firm-wide posting activity. Firms also adjust the type of employment relationship they seek to establish, shifting away from full-time, non-internship postings in states with greater UI tax exposure. Reallocation effects are stronger when separation costs are more salient and firms have greater geographic flexibility. Evidence from Title XII borrowing during the COVID-19 period further supports the interpretation that firms reallocate hiring across states when expected separation costs rise. A greater tilt in job postings toward lower-separation-cost states is associated with higher market valuation but lower short-run profitability and operating efficiency, highlighting how managerial discretion over internal hiring allocation can shape firms’ exposure to workforce-related risk and firm outcomes.

detail.abstract: AI is creating wider impact in healthcare by accelerating diagnosis through accurate analysis of medical images, supporting personalized treatments through precision medicine and faster drug discovery. It also improves efficiency by automating administrative tasks and facilitates proactive care through predictive analytics, remote monitoring, and telehealth. While AI in healthcare is promising on above fronts, it also faces challenges such as regulatory alignment, data quality issues, integration with existing systems, collaboration with healthcare professionals, privacy and security concerns, ethical considerations, and real-time data processing. detail.abstract: Since 2019 consumption in Spain has increased less than income and the saving rate has risen. This article analyses households' marginal propensity to consume and its potential contribution to the change in the saving rate. Takeaways • Marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is estimated in the Survey of Financial Competences (ECF by its Spanish initials) and the Spanish Survey of Household Finances (EFF by its Spanish initials) by the response to the following question: "What percentage of a lottery prize equal to one month's income would you spend over the following 12 months?". • Compared with its pre-pandemic levels, MPC has fallen in Spain in recent years. title: Macroeconomic Developments in Canada: From the COVID-19 Recession to Economic Slowdown (2019-2025)

detail.title: Macroeconomic Developments in Canada: From the COVID-19 Recession to Economic Slowdown (2019-2025)
detail.abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic developments in Canada from the COVID-19 recession to the subsequent period of economic slowdown between 2019 and 2025. The study analyzes how the Canadian economy responded to one of the most severe economic shocks in modern history through a combination of expansionary fiscal policy and accommodative monetary policy, followed by an aggressive monetary tightening cycle aimed at restoring price stability. Using data from Statistics Canada, the Bank of Canada, the OECD, FRED, and other official sources, the paper evaluates changes in key macroeconomic indicators, including real GDP, inflation, unemployment, investment, household debt, government expenditure, external trade, and interest rates. The analysis shows that emergency fiscal support and highly accommodative monetary policy played a crucial role in stabilizing economic activity during the pandemic and supporting the post-pandemic recovery. However, these policies also contributed to inflationary pressures that required rapid policy tightening beginning in 2022. The study further demonstrates how higher interest rates weakened household consumption, housing activity, and business investment, while structural challenges such as weak productivity growth, high household indebtedness, and dependence on commodity exports continued to constrain Canada's long-term economic performance. Overall, the paper highlights the policy trade-off between maintaining price stability and sustaining economic growth in a small and open advanced economy.

detail.abstract: We develop and estimate an open economy DSGE model for the euro area in which imported energy, priced in foreign currency, enters both consumption and production. Global energy prices and the exchange rate therefore jointly determine domestic inflation. We find that energy and exchange-rate disturbances account for the bulk of short-run volatility in headline euro area inflation, with energy price shocks driving most of the post-pandemic surge. Because energy and non-energy goods are poor substitutes, an adverse energy price shock raises import values, deteriorating the trade balance and depreciating the real exchange rate through the net-foreign-asset and UIP channels. The exchange-rate channel strengthens monetary transmission and improves the short-run inflation-output trade-off relative to a non-energy economy. Optimal policy can exploit this channel rather than looking through energy price shocks. However, the case for looking through such shocks becomes stronger when the central bank assigns a greater weight to output gap stabilization and prices become stickier.

detail.abstract: Severe weather volatility continues to impose escalating risks on public safety, municipal infrastructure, and regional economies across the United States. While extensive climate and hazard datasets exist-particularly through the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Storm Events Database-their complexity often prevents timely, actionable interpretation by the diverse stakeholders responsible for emergency response. Using a historical baseline of Georgia's severe weather records from 2014-2016, this white paper proposes a Multi-Tiered Communication Architecture to translate raw storm data into tailored, user-appropriate insights for three distinct audiences: state executives, emergency management agencies (EMAs), and the general public. Using Georgia's severe weather records as a case study, the framework demonstrates how differentiated data granularity, visualization design, and communication modalities can improve strategic planning, operational decision-making, and community readiness. The architecture integrates aggregated economic loss analyses, interactive spatial-temporal dashboards, and simpli ied public-facing safety materials. Findings reveal over $71.71 million in economic liabilities, concentrated regional vulnerabilities, and seasonal patterns that require targeted resource allocation. Ultimately, this white paper provides a scalable model for transforming climate data into a structured decision-support ecosystem, enabling more ef icient governance, improved emergency response, and enhanced public safety outcomes.

detail.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with the surface code requires a classical decoder that returns a correction in less than one syndrome extraction round-a latency budget of approximately 1 µs on superconducting hardware that is below what software decoders achieve and at the edge of what FPGA and GPU implementations report. We present tt-qec-predecoder, an end-to-end pre-decoder system targeting this regime by mapping a selective-scan statespace model (Mamba/S6) onto the Tenstorrent Blackhole RISC-V tensor architecture, combined with a hardware-resident integrity and formal-verification pipeline. The decoder is a 16 Mparameter Sparse Mamba network whose recurrence has O(k) work in k, the number of non-trivial syndrome bits, executed as a tile-resident Tensix kernel with no host roundtrip. Around the kernel we build a Z3-based proof framework that discharges five abstract safety obligations (no NoC deadlock, no buffer overflow, worst-case latency bound, fixedpoint quantizer error bound, no-op safety), a BLAKE3 contentaddressed integrity chain (QCIVET) covering every artifact from training data to deployed weights, and a standardized benchmarking suite (qec-lego-bench) for like-for-like comparison against PyMatching (CPU), Micro Blossom (FPGA), and NVIDIA Ising (GPU) baselines at code distances d ∈ {3, 5, 7, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 32}. We describe the architecture, the kernel design and its hardware-aware Taylor-approximated discretization, the verification methodology and its current limitations, and the benchmarking framework. We additionally report a first round of experimental validation: measured CPU baselines on the FP32 dense reference model, Blackhole latencies projected from those baselines through a published scaling chain (INT4 quantization, tensor-core SIMD, Tenstorrent NoC streaming), an end-to-end decode run on the IBM Quantum cloud simulator, and-as a new empirical result-50,000 shots of raw complexvalued IQ syndrome data harvested from a real IBM Heron R2 processor (ibm_fez) via the IBM Quantum open plan. Realhardware Blackhole validation remains explicitly pending. Source code is available under AGPL-3.0-or-later.

detail.abstract: Modern AI systems are becoming powerful task performers, but they are not yet reliable capability-evolution infrastructures. They can answer questions, retrieve knowledge, use tools, coordinate agents, exhibit emergent or newly observable capabilities, and complete multi-step workflows. Yet a central engineering gap remains: task success, model outputs, tool calls, failures, feedback, validation results, boundary revisions, and governance actions do not automatically become reusable, verifiable, governed, rollbackable, and evolvable platform capabilities. As a result, many current AI systems can perform increasingly complex tasks while still lacking a stable infrastructure for accumulating capability over time. This paper proposes the AGI Foundation Platform (AFP), a model-agnostic conceptual and architectural framework for organizing heterogeneous capability sources into an evolvable capability infrastructure. AFP treats models, tools, data, documents, expert workflows, evidence records, validation results, feedback, and governance rules as materials for a governed capability lifecycle rather than as isolated components. At its core, the Cognitive Evolution Backbone (CEB) transforms these materials into capability objects, Minimal Capability Units, evidence boundaries, validation states, negative-result evidence, runtime snapshots, permission states, version traces, and evolutionary memory. The framework further introduces three complementary mechanisms. Boundary Exploration and Hypothesis Generation generates constrained candidates from gaps, failures, weak signals, feedback deviations, negative-result evidence, anomaly signals, and cross-domain boundaries. Adversarial Validation and Path Optimization compresses these candidates into reliability states through counterexample search, perturbation testing, boundary stress testing, causal calibration, evidence comparison, reality calibration, and path comparison. Graded Autonomy and Controlled Evolution governs whether candidate updates should be recorded, observed, sandboxed, reweighted, released, frozen, rolled back, replaced, archived, or escalated to human judgment, expert review, or external audit. The paper also defines a Minimum Viable AFP (MV-AFP) as a practical starting point: a bounded platform instance that preserves the full capability-evolution loop under limited scope, limited automation, limited validation depth, and conservative governance. From MV-AFP, the framework outlines a path toward scalable capability networks, distributed AFP, and eventually an Evolvable Socio-Cognitive Network (ESCN). By treating failure, criticism, contradiction, boundary breakdown, and negative results as evidence for capability evolution rather than as mere errors or peripheral records, AFP offers a framework-level path for making AGI-oriented capability evolution startable, testable, governable, rollbackable, transferable, and scalable under current technical and organizational conditions.
