detail.abstract: AFIR sets a single regulatory floor across all 27 EU member states, but a CPO that achieves full compliance in its home market is not compliant in the next one. This paper maps a four-layer compliance stack, EU baseline obligations, national transposition instruments, hardware protocol variance, and DSO connection queues, that compounds non-linearly as growth-phase charge point operators expand cross-border. Drawing on a composite 200 to 500 charger operator profile and concrete country-pair analysis across the Netherlands, Germany, Spain, and Portugal, the paper introduces a Regulatory Maturity Classification that sorts national instruments by whether they solve a current EU-wide problem, a future one, or one already superseded by EU standards. It quantifies the financial consequence: carry costs, hardware recertification delays, and a utilisation timing mismatch that compress investor returns below standard acquisition assumptions, and shows how this drives market consolidation toward large operators able to absorb compliance cost as overhead while growth-phase entrants retreat to markets they already understand, a pattern that runs directly counter to AFIR's deployment objectives. The paper closes with three recommendations for the AFIR mandatory review, open for public consultation through 3 August 2026: consolidating non-binding Article 5 guidance into binding technical standards, establishing a single EU-level EVSE hardware type approval registry, and mandating a minimum OCPP version with built-in forward compatibility, the last independently corroborated by CharIN's own submission to the same review.

title: Peripheral Attention Engineering: Structured Peripheral Context Improves LLM Decision Quality
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Peripheral Attention Engineering: Structured Peripheral Context Improves LLM Decision Quality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of A.I. Plus Automation, which develops AI consulting tools. No external funding, grants, or competing financial interests exist that could have influenced this research.

detail.abstract: Large language models answer queries using directly relevant material, but they lack the lateral, situational context a competent human consults silently before responding. This paper introduces Peripheral Attention Engineering (PAE): the deliberate structuring and provision of unrequested-but-decision-relevant context to shape LLM responses. A controlled within-subjects experiment across four domains (customer service, medical triage, legal advisory, financial advisory; N=500 total scenarios) and six conditions tests whether structured peripheral context improves response quality when controlling for token count, domain relevance, and prompt structure. Results confirm all preregistered hypotheses: peripheral context produces large gains in response quality (baseline mean=1.63-2.06 vs anomaly-flagged mean=4.01-4.90 on a 5-point scale, Cohen's d=2.02-3.10, all p<0.0001); the improvement is attributable to informational content, not prompt length (noise d=0.04, n.s.) or domain relevance (expanded direct d=0.06, n.s.); slot-structured context outperforms equivalent unstructured context (d=0.13, p<0.0001); and the effect generalizes across three model families and all four domains. A Phase 2 fine-tuning experiment demonstrates that contextual reach-the unprompted instinct to retrieve peripheral context before answering-is trainable, with a fine-tuned Gemma 4 12B model achieving 100% context-request and context-use rates, and outperforming all Phase 1 generators on the full benchmark. A knowledge-graph substrate (Phase 3) and a practical Python library (pae.context.wrap()) are released as open-source artifacts.

title: Distributional Rank-Rank Regression for Heterogeneous Dependence
affiliations: Keio University and Seoul National University - School of Economics

detail.title: Distributional Rank-Rank Regression for Heterogeneous Dependence
detail.abstract: Intergenerational mobility, the extent to which economic status evolves across generations, is central to understanding economic opportunity and social dynamics. Rankrank regression has become the standard tool for measuring intergenerational mobility through a linear relationship, but it may overlook heterogeneous dependence patterns. We introduce distributional rank-rank regression, which provides rank-specific correlations across the distribution of parent and child outcomes. Drawing on quantile-based correlation techniques, our framework comprehensively captures nonlinear mobility patterns, accommodates noncontinuous outcome variables through generalized ranks, and incorporates observed covariates via conditional ranks. We establish the asymptotic properties of the estimator under potential misspecification of the first-stage conditional distributions and propose bootstrap procedures for inference. An empirical application to intergenerational educational mobility in India illustrates the proposed method.

title: From Shades to Traits: Integrating Color-Based Personality Inference into Destination Recommender System
affiliations: National Central University

detail.title: From Shades to Traits: Integrating Color-Based Personality Inference into Destination Recommender System
detail.abstract: Destination Recommender Systems (DRSs) are designed to assist tourists in identifying suitable destinations. Traditional DRSs analyze the sites that users and similar users have visited to recommend destinations. However, such approaches overlook the findings from trait theory, which indicate that personality traits can influence user preferences for various items and tourism destinations. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this research is the first to verify this theory using state-of-the-art recommender algorithms, such as collaborative filtering approaches enhanced with GCN and mass diffusion enhanced with an attention mechanism. The results show that incorporating personality traits into these methodologies significantly improves the precision and recall of recommendations. However, requesting personality traits may be perceived as intrusive by some users. This study, therefore, proposes using color psychology to analyze personality traits from the dominant colors of user photos shared on social media. As a result, an ensemble classifier is designed to predict user personality traits based on dominant colors extracted from ten scenic photos. These personality traits are then applied to a mass diffusion-based recommender system. The results show that the proposed CPRS (Color Personality-enriched Recommender Systems) outperforms state-of-the-art personality-enriched DRSs by a wide margin.

title: Governing Openness without Moderation: Evidence from a Decentralized Platform
affiliations: ,  and Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University

detail.title: Governing Openness without Moderation: Evidence from a Decentralized Platform
detail.abstract: User-generated content (UGC) platforms sustain openness through ex post governance mechanisms such as moderation, exclusion, and centralized intervention. Yet, these mechanisms become constrained in decentralized UGC platforms, where decision rights are distributed and harmful contributions are difficult to reverse or remove. This study examines how increased openness affects platform outcomes when ex post governance is infeasible, and how decentralized governance mechanisms shape these effects. We exploit a sudden policy change on Mirror.xyz, a decentralized UGC platform, that removed pre-screening and opened publishing rights to all users. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that increased openness expands content diversity but also increases content toxicity. We further show that pre-screening with decentralized community voting mitigates these quality deteriorations, suggesting that collective pre-screening can function as an effective ex ante governance mechanism when centralized moderation is limited. In contrast, peer incentives generate unintended consequences: contributors with higher rewards become less exploratory and more likely to produce toxic content. This indicates that incentives can amplify the risks of openness. This study contributes to platform governance research by showing how decentralization shifts governance from ex post intervention to ex ante governance mechanisms. More broadly, the findings reveal the challenges of maintaining openness when centralized enforcement is structurally constrained.

title: Towards Self-Evolving Ontologies: A Dynamic Approach for Automated Construction and Real-Time Adaptation to Data Changes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Towards Self-Evolving Ontologies: A Dynamic Approach for Automated Construction and Real-Time Adaptation to Data Changes
detail.abstract: The rapid growth and variability of data require ontologies to be constructed in a way that allows them to evolve continuously, ensuring their relevance and usefulness. This paper proposes a novel method to automatically construct ontologies from the start, capable of detecting changes in the underlying data and continuously updating in response to these changes. By integrating real-time data monitoring, automated change detection, and efficient updating mechanisms, we address current limitations in ontology management. We apply this approach across multiple domains—Protein, Civic, Virus, and Herbal Ontologies—demonstrating its scalability and effectiveness in real-world datasets. The results show significant improvements in the ontology’s complexity and accuracy during real-time monitoring, highlighting the success of our dynamic ontology construction method.The proposed approach aims to enhance the adaptability and usability of ontologies in dynamic environments, with significant implications for semantic web technologies, artificial intelligence, and data integration systems.

title: Regulating Attention in Digital Platforms via Dynamic Taxation and Strategic Learning
affiliations: , , ,  and

detail.title: Regulating Attention in Digital Platforms via Dynamic Taxation and Strategic Learning

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported in part by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Institute of Food and Agriculture (USDA NIFA), under award number 2023‑68012‑39076.

detail.abstract: We study the problem of mitigating information overload in large-scale digital ecosystems through dynamically learned taxation mechanisms. We model the interaction between a social planner and strategic message senders as a Stackelberg game, where the planner (leader) sets a tax policy on messaging, and the senders (followers) adapt their behavior over time. To capture realistic dynamics, we represent the system as a Markov game in which senders learn approximate best responses via reinforcement learning under limited interaction horizons, giving rise to non-equilibrium and boundedly rational behavior. The social planner’s objective balances two competing goals: reducing aggregate message volume to alleviate information overload and promoting equity in access to user attention across senders. We formalize these objectives using a combination of message volume penalties and inequality measures such as the Gini coefficient. Leveraging a query-based follower oracle, we show that the leader’s policy optimization problem can be cast as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), enabling the use of reinforcement learning methods to search over tax policies. We develop a simulation framework that incorporates realistic features, including budget constraints, stochastic utility patterns, and limited attention capacity. Through computational experiments, we provide preliminary evidence that adaptive tax policies can influence message volume and allocation in simplified environments. At the same time, our results reveal important challenges in dynamic settings, including instability, non-convergence, and the emergence of degenerate equilibria driven by learning dynamics. These findings highlight a key insight: policy design in attention-constrained environments must account for the adaptive and non-equilibrium responses of strategic agents. While taxation offers a principled mechanism for regulating information flow, its effectiveness depends critically on the interaction between incentives and learning.

title: A Study on Customer Behaviour Towards Online Shopping
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Galgotias University

detail.title: A Study on Customer Behaviour Towards Online Shopping
detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to understand customer behavior in online shopping. The research includes responses from 50 participants, comprising both men and women, selected through convenient sampling. As the internet rapidly becomes a global phenomenon, it is transforming how people shop and purchase goods and services. Many businesses have adopted the internet to reduce their marketing expenses, which in turn lowers the prices of their goods and services. They also use it to sell their products, communicate with customers, obtain feedback, and survey customer satisfaction. Online shopping is one of the many ways consumers use the internet; they also use it to compare product features, prices, and after-sales services provided by different retailers. Specialists remain optimistic about the future of internet business. Consumer behavior in online shopping has become a focal point of research as e-commerce markets evolve. This study reviews literature on online consumer behavior, exploring theoretical frameworks, empirical studies, and regional perspectives. Key themes include factors influencing online purchase decisions, such as convenience, trust, and perceived risk, and the role of cultural differences in shaping consumer attitudes toward e-commerce. Comparative research highlights variations in online shopping behavior across different countries, providing insights into global e-commerce trends. The review emphasizes the importance of understanding the nuances of online consumer behavior for businesses navigating the complex landscape of e-commerce markets and identifies avenues for future research.

title: A Qualitative Phenomenological Study of Emergency Response Resilience in Island Contexts
affiliations: University of the Cumberlands

detail.title: A Qualitative Phenomenological Study of Emergency Response Resilience in Island Contexts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could be perceived as influencing this research. The author is an independent researcher conducting this doctoral dissertation at the University of the Cumberlands with no external funding or commercial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research was approved by the University of the Cumberlands Institutional Review Board (IRB) prior to data collection. Informed consent was obtained from all 20 emergency responder participants. Participants (nurses, police officers, paramedics, and rescue personnel) were fully informed of the research objectives, methodology, and their right to withdraw at any time. All ethical guidelines were strictly adhered to throughout the study.
declarations.funderStatement: This doctoral dissertation was conducted as part of the Ph.D. in Information Technology at the University of the Cumberlands. The research was not funded by any external grants, government agencies, or private organizations. All research was completed using institutional resources and the author's own resources.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This is a qualitative phenomenological study, not a clinical trial. No clinical trial registration is required for this research.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this qualitative phenomenological study was to explore the lived experiences of emergency responders in Puerto Rico as they managed technological and infrastructural disruptions during multi-hazard events. Emergency responders in island regions face unique challenges related to fragile infrastructure, limited system redundancy, and repeated exposure to disasters, yet limited research has examined how responders experience and adapt to these conditions. Guided by Resilience Theory and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, this study addressed four research questions: responders’ experiences with system failures, decision making, and coordination during digital disruptions; adaptive resilience practices; and the characteristics of emergency information systems perceived as effective. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 20 emergency responders representing diverse professional roles, including law enforcement, healthcare, emergency medical services, and rescue leadership. Using phenomenological analysis procedures, the interview transcripts were coded and analyzed to identify shared themes that reflected participants’ experiences. The findings revealed that responders relied heavily on human adaptability, improvisation, analog tools, community support, and flexible decision-making to maintain operational continuity during system failures. Participants also identified the importance of pre-established communication plans, interagency collaboration, and redundant tools in supporting effective response. The study’s findings contribute to a deeper understanding of emergency response within infrastructure-constrained environments and offer implications for improving emergency management practices, system design, and future research focused on resilience and socio-technical adaptation in disaster-prone regions.

title: When the Nearest Driver Loses: Order Allocation as Incentive Design in Ride-Hailing
affiliations: Renmin University of China, School of Business and Renmin University of China, School of Business

detail.title: When the Nearest Driver Loses: Order Allocation as Incentive Design in Ride-Hailing
detail.abstract: This paper studies the hidden dispatch rule using 3.94 million ride-hailing transactions and 538 million GPS pings from a large Chinese city. We reconstruct feasible candidate drivers immediately before dispatch and compare the selected driver with rejected feasible alternatives for the same passenger request. The closest feasible driver receives the order in only 10.45\% of valid events, although pickup distance remains strongly penalized. Assignment also depends on driver's idle/in-trip status. For the platform assigning a given order, a driver's recent activity on that platform raises assignment probability, while recent activity on other platforms lowers it. This contrast identifies platform-specific priority rather than a generic activity premium. The rule is also contestability-dependent: drivers more attached to the assigning platform receive higher baseline access, while multihoming drivers receive stronger marginal rewards for recent activity on assigning-platform; lower-share platforms rely more on this activity margin. Machine-learning validation confirms that distance, driver state, and platform-specific activity improve winner ranking in hold-out choice sets. The findings provide direct order-level evidence on allocation primitives that ride-hailing models typically assume and show that dispatch algorithms allocate priority over earning opportunities by combining pickup efficiency, driver engagement, and platform attachment.

title: Centrality-Entropy Scheduling for Energy-Efficient AI Data Centers
affiliations: University of the Cumberlands

detail.title: Centrality-Entropy Scheduling for Energy-Efficient AI Data Centers
detail.abstract: As AI infrastructure becomes power-constrained, the scheduler increasingly determines not only efficiency but operational resilience. Conventional cluster schedulers optimize for utilization, job completion time, or raw energy, and a growing body of work optimizes energy or carbon directly, each objective pursued in isolation. This leaves an unmanaged tradeoff between efficiency and reliability, with a hidden failure mode: aggressive energy minimization consolidates load onto the fewest active nodes, which lowers idle power but concentrates thermal load, raises the risk of service-level violations, and induces oscillatory rescheduling as the controller repeatedly packs and unpacks hot nodes. This paper introduces an energyweighted Centrality-Entropy Index (CEI) that treats consolidation, allocation diversity, and power cost as a single governed objective rather than competing afterthoughts. The formulation exposes a principled tradeoff parameter between energy efficiency and operational resilience, recovering pure bin-packing and pure spread placement as limiting cases, and it incorporates time-varying grid carbon intensity to support carbon-aware placement. We evaluate the approach in a trace-driven simulation calibrated to published per-node power figures, on a mix of GPU inference and training workloads, against bin-packing, spread, default Kubernetes, energy-only, and carbon-only baselines. At a governed operating point the method matches the energy and carbon of single-objective optimizers while reducing their service-level violations by three to four times, and it lowers scheduling oscillation by more than an order of magnitude relative to greedy energy minimization. We further validate the scheduler against a live Kubernetes control plane, confirming correct binding and that the governance weight changes consolidation as designed, and we release the scheduler and benchmark to support reproducibility. More broadly, we frame energy-resilience governance, making the efficiencyreliability tradeoff an explicit and tunable decision, as an emerging design principle for powerconstrained AI infrastructure, of which the data center scheduler is the first and most pressing instance.

title: A Theory of Cash in the 21st Century
affiliations: University of Granada - Department of Economic Theory and History

detail.title: A Theory of Cash in the 21st Century
detail.abstract:
Cash — physical currency in the form of banknotes and coins — is commonly treated
in contemporary economics as a declining, inconvenient, and even socially harmful
legacy technology. This paper argues the contrary. Drawing on monetary theory from
Menger (1892), Minsky (1986), and Feinig (2022) to Mehrling (2012), on the political
theory of money from Desan (2014) and Pistor (2019) to Eich (2022), on sociology from
Simmel (1900) to Zelizer (1994) and Dodd (2014), on behavioral economics from Prelec
and Loewenstein (1998) to Shah, Eisenkraft, Bettman, and Chartrand (2016), on
constitutional theory from Warren and Brandeis (1890) to the CJEU's Hessischer
Rundfunk decision (2021), and on new evidence from the April 2025 Iberian Peninsula
blackout, the Ukraine war, and Nordic total-defence doctrines, this paper advances an
integrated theory of cash as a sovereign monetary institution for the twenty-first century.

     The paper makes seven original contributions. First, it situates cash within Mehrling's
(2012) money hierarchy as the uniquely accessible Tier-1 public liability of the modern
state — the only form of central-bank money directly available to citizens. Second, it
demonstrates that the canonical economic functions of money are performed by cash in
qualitatively distinct ways that no digital substitute replicates, including a documented
pain-of-paying discipline (Prelec and Simester, 2001) that digital abstraction
systematically destroys. Third, following Zelizer (1994), Dodd (2014), Hart (1986), and
Simmel (1900), the paper argues that cash carries irreducible social meanings as a vehicle
for earmarking, trust, solidarity, and inclusion. Fourth, drawing on Garratt and van Oordt
(2021) and Kahn, McAndrews, and Roberds (2005), it argues that the transactional
anonymity cash provides functions as a privacy-preserving public good — in the formal
sense of Garratt and van Oordt (2021) — even though cash itself, as privately held
sovereign money, is neither non-rival nor non-excludable. Fifth, engaging the political
turn in monetary theory (Eich, 2022; Pistor, 2019; Desan, 2014), it argues that cash is a
constitutional technology whose erosion constitutes a political change — the progressive
privatization of monetary access — that is occurring without democratic deliberation.
Sixth, it reconstructs the historical arc of cash from the constitutional monetary debates
of the School of Salamanca through the Nixon shock and the neoliberal era, arguing that
the 'death of cash' narrative is not a technical inevitability but the culmination of a
decades-long project of monetary depoliticization. Seventh, it argues that the geopolitical
context of the 2020s has made cash not less but far more important as a resilience asset,
a sovereignty instrument, and a structural check on private monetary power.

     The paper concludes that the persistence of cash — paradoxically rising in aggregate
circulation even as its transactional share declines — is not an anomaly to be explained
away but a rational collective response to systemic risk. Cash is not a relic. It is, in the
precise language of political economy, an institution — and its most important dimension,
insufficiently theorized until now, is not transactional but constitutional: it is the last form
of money that citizens can own, hold, and use as a matter of private right, without
institutional intermediation, without digital surveillance, and without permission.

title: The Mirror-Image Paradigm: Endogenous Ambiguity and Macroeconomic Entropy Rejection
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice

detail.title: The Mirror-Image Paradigm: Endogenous Ambiguity and Macroeconomic Entropy Rejection
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a novel foundational framework for macroeconomic dynamics—the Mirror Image Paradigm—which endogenizes deep structural ambiguity as a thermodynamic-like projection of aggregate micro-level complexity. Standard macro-finance frameworks (DSGE, New Keynesian, and robust control implementations) generate aggregate fluctuations by routing exogenous, uninterpretable structural shocks (ϵt) through passive linear engineering systems. We invert this epistemology. We prove that the aggregate system’s volatility is an endogenous 

feedback loop: agents generate local financial and contractual complexity (ki,t) to hedge idiosyncratic risks, yet the general equilibrium aggregation of these optimization strategies (Kt) fundamentally distorts the global topology of the state space. By linking the Kullback-Leibler divergence bound directly to Kt, we overcome the known micro-foundational limits of posterior-based informational costs in endogenous equilibrium settings. As the economy approaches an endogenous attention and computational threshold (K∗), the shadow price of model misspecification diverges to negative infinity. This induces a sharp, non-linear phase transition—a coordinated dynamic contraction defined as systemic entropy rejection. We provide the axiomatic and operational blueprints for a pure endogenous theory of financial crises and business cycles.

title: On Moneyness: An Infrastructural View

detail.title: On Moneyness: An Infrastructural View
detail.abstract: Moneyness is a matter of degree, varying both across things and over time. A theory of moneyness is needed to explain this and guide normative reflection on existing monetary systems and reform proposals. I reject both the market view and the state view of moneyness in favour of an infrastructural view: low volatility and high liquidity jointly constitute moneyness, both endowed by infrastructural reality. This explains various historical and contemporary monetary phenomena and diagnoses the errors of two camps of heterodox monetary theory: the deprivatisation/modern monetary theory camp and the decentralisation/digital-metallism camp.

title: Denied: Racial Disparities in Insurance Claims
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management (IIMB), Bangalore, Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Finance,  and University of South Florida - Muma College of Business

detail.title: Denied: Racial Disparities in Insurance Claims
detail.abstract: We document that Black homeowners receive less value from their insurance policies than White homeowners with similar coverage. Using detailed administrative data on policies and claims, we find that Black policyholders face higher claim rejection rates, lower payouts, and longer resolution times than White policyholders filing similar claims in similar locations. Insurance agents contribute to these disparities, with the gap disappearing for Black agents. Disparities are larger where competitive and economic constraints on agents are weaker. Our findings show that racial gaps in financial markets extend beyond the point of sale, affecting wealth preservation, not just accumulation.

title: Civic Engagement Rate (CER): A Counterfactual Framework for Measuring Participatory Mobilization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Civic Engagement Rate (CER): A Counterfactual Framework for Measuring Participatory Mobilization
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Civic Engagement Rate (CER), a multidimensional framework for measuring civic mobilization within participatory governance systems. Existing participation indicators often capture isolated forms of engagement such as electoral turnout, digital interaction, or episodic consultation, while failing to distinguish between temporary activation, symbolic participation, and sustained civic involvement. CER addresses this limitation by conceptualizing civic engagement as a composite territorial phenomenon combining breadth of participation, depth of involvement, and temporal persistence. The framework additionally incorporates representativeness across social and demographic groups, distinguishing broad societal mobilization from participation concentrated within narrow activist segments. Methodologically, CER employs a non-substitutable geometric aggregation structure and integrates counterfactual evaluation logic through difference-indifferences comparison designs. The paper defines the conceptual structure of CER, proposes operational measurement procedures, and discusses validity threats associated with participation measurement. Although initially developed within a broader governance coordination research program, CER is presented here as a standalone methodology applicable across participatory governance, deliberative democracy, civic consultation, and public coordination initiatives. The framework is operationalized through behavioral and survey indicators and is designed for longitudinal and counterfactual analysis using difference-indifferences logic.

title: The Deposit Base -  Multibanking and Bank Stability
affiliations: Catholic University of Portugal (UCP) - Catolica Lisbon School of Business and Economics and University of Bonn - Economic Science Area

detail.title: The Deposit Base -  Multibanking and Bank Stability
detail.abstract: To provide maturity transformation, banks need a deposit base -- deposits that could be, but are typically not, withdrawn and are therefore available for long-term investments. We show that a larger deposit base reduces a bank's vulnerability to panic runs. When depositors maintain multiple accounts across banks, the allocation of the deposit base becomes endogenous, creating externalities that affect run probabilities. We analyze the effect of multibanking on financial stability and demonstrate that in an economy with heterogeneous institutions, households allocate inefficiently low funds to maturity-transforming banks due to this deposit base externality. This has implications for financial stability in the context of Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs), regulatory ring-fencing, and long-term saving subsidies.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-91
title: The Effect of Reminders for Self-Set Goals on Productivity
affiliations: Bowdoin College, , University of Chicago and Precision Development (PxD)

detail.title: The Effect of Reminders for Self-Set Goals on Productivity

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-91
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how reminders for self-set goals influence productivity by analyzing data from 10,187 volunteer agricultural extension workers in Rwanda. We elicited workers' goals and experimentally varied their salience through text reminders. Due to unforeseen logistical delays, approximately half of the treatment group received reminders after completing their tasks. We find that goal reminders received during the regular working period increased a productivity index by 0.08 standard deviations, while reminders sent late had no effect. Further analysis of heterogeneity by goal ambition quartiles reveals an inverted U-shaped relationship: reminders are effective for goals in the second and third quartiles, but ineffective for low or excessively high goals. These results suggest that workers who set ambitious yet realistic goals are more likely to respond to reminders and increase productivity, consistent with prior evidence on externally set goals.

title: Road Networks and Tropical Deforestation
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, School of Business and Economics and IPAG Business School

detail.title: Road Networks and Tropical Deforestation
detail.abstract: We analyze a dynamic spatial model of deforestation in which roads facilitate agricultural expansion. The model's key innovation is that road construction costs decrease with the existing road stock, creating positive network externalities that are specific to infrastructure: each road built serves as a stepping stone for further road construction. Under open access, myopic producers fail to internalize that roads built today facilitate future road construction. As a result, the pace of deforestation is faster under a forward-looking regime of private property than open access, reversing a standard result from resource economics. We calibrate the model to the Brazilian Amazon, where cattle ranching is the primary driver of deforestation, and calculate the international transfer required to incentivize Brazil to implement a carbon tax that completely stops deforestation. We find that Brazil's extensive existing road network increases this required transfer, demonstrating how infrastructure creates ``deforestation lock-in'' that makes conservation progressively more expensive.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-92
title: Leaning Against Inflation Experiences
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Leaning Against Inflation Experiences

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-92
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: A large share of secular variation in real interest rates can be understood as the effect of monetary policy leaning against experience-based long-run inflation expectations. Survey microdata show that adaptive learning from experienced inflation generates highly persistent, slow-moving longrun inflation expectations. When expectations are shaped by experience, central banks cannot anchor them through communication. Instead, when expectations deviate from the inflation target, monetary policy must remain persistently hawkish or dovish to generate realized inflation outcomes that, through agents' belief updating, gradually pull long-run expectations back toward the target. Consistent with this mechanism, I find a strong positive relationship between experience-based long-run inflation expectations and real interest rates in the U.S., Germany, the U.K., and Japan. Under their subjective expectations, private-sector agents do not anticipate future reversals in inflation and short-term real interest rates. As a result, long-term real interest rates move with experience-based long-run inflation expectations about as much as short-term real interest rates do, consistent with the data. Secular movements in real rates are also accompanied by persistent patterns in interest-rate forecast errors. Overall, the interaction of monetary policy and learning from experience generates a distinct source of secular real-rate variation, beyond movements in the natural rate of interest.

reference: European Corporate Governance Institute – Finance Working Paper No. 1145/2026
title: Ownership Structures and Sustainability in Big Tech Firms
affiliations: Tilburg University - School of Law; European Banking Center (EBC) and University of Applied Sciences Wiener Neustadt

detail.title: Ownership Structures and Sustainability in Big Tech Firms

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute – Finance Working Paper No. 1145/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Finance Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: In this paper, we examine the association between institutional ownership, common ownership, ownership concentration and ESG performance among major publicly traded technology firms. Using a panel of 14 large technology companies over the period 2004–2025, we combine ESG, ownership, and financial data to investigate whether sustainability outcomes are associated with ownership by the largest institutional investors, ownership concentration, and common ownership structures. We find that ownership by the Big Three asset managers is unrelated to ESG performance once firm and year fixed effects are included. However, broader ownership by the largest institutional investors, measured using a Big Four ownership variable, is positively associated with ESG outcomes across multiple specifications. We also find that ownership concentration and common ownership exhibit negative associations with several ESG measures, particularly environmental and emissions-related outcomes. The findings indicate that ownership identity and ownership structure represent distinct governance channels with different implications for sustainability outcomes.

title: The Odyssey of Third Country Removal
affiliations: University of Kentucky - J. David Rosenberg College of Law

detail.title: The Odyssey of Third Country Removal
detail.abstract:
This essay discusses the case of one individual, Kilmar Ábrego García, and how his story exemplifies the odyssey into which many noncitizens have been cast during the first year of the second Trump administration. Specifically, this essay focuses on the amplified use of third country removals as part of a mass deportation campaign. This essay sounds the alarm that these third country removals are likely to become more expansive because of the rapidity of the removal process, the vulnerability of affected populations, and the unwillingness of courts to intervene after the fact. 

 

Third country removals, as they currently function, pose a real threat to noncitizens and citizens alike. Despite former Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) Secretary Kristi Noem’s protestations that no U.S. citizens have been detained or arrested, instances of such conduct number into the hundreds during the first year of the second Trump administration.

 

Past administrations have also, by error, arrested, detained, and deported U.S. citizens. Because the present process provides a singular mechanism to prevent removal—asserting fear of removal to a specific place—with no review, an asylum officer or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”) officer is frequently the only person who stands between an individual and removal.24 Under the current administration, pressure on officers, immigration judges, and Board of Immigration Appeals (“BIA”) judges has eroded any remaining confidence that these officials employed by the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”) or DHS could act in a neutral fashion as arbiters and independent decision makers.

 

Despite these obstacles, local communities have been steadily intervening to help prevent detentions of their noncitizen neighbors, and legal actors have been successfully employing various forms of litigation to push back on these efforts. There may yet be a resistance that can adequately respond to these draconian measures.

reference: Liberty Street Economics
title: Liquidity Fades as Treasuries Age
affiliations: , Federal Reserve Banks, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, , Independent and Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Liquidity Fades as Treasuries Age

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
More than $30 trillion U.S. Treasury debt is outstanding. Less than 4 percent of this amount, which is associated with the most recently issued Treasuries, called on-the-run securities, accounts for 65 percent of average daily trading volume. The remaining portion of the amount outstanding is accounted for by seasoned issues that have been replaced by newer benchmarks, which are referred to as off-the-run securities. In this post, we review the key results in our paper that uses transaction-level Treasury TRACE data to study how trading activity and liquidity evolve as securities move from on-the-run to off-the-run. We show three main patterns. First, off-the-run notes and bonds rely much more on dealer-to-customer intermediation than benchmark securities. Second, trading activity falls sharply and transaction costs increase as securities age. Third, securities that are cheapest to deliver into Treasury futures are an important exception: they trade more actively than other off-the-run bonds of similar age.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates Korea's tariff elasticity using 2014 transaction-level customs data covering about 7.5 million import records from 230 exporters and 10,557 HS10 products. Using the structural gravity framework of Fontagné et al. (2022), we employ PPML with alternative fixed-effect structures to address endogeneity. Elasticities differ across products: consumer goods are highly elastic, homogeneous goods such as minerals display very large elasticities, and several HS sections show no significant estimates. These results highlight substantial heterogeneity across products and the risks of relying on a single aggregate elasticity. We also show that non-tariff trade costs matter: freight and insurance charges vary more than tariffs and remain strongly elastic under extensive fixed effects. detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of the widening interest rate differential between Korea and the U.S. on the won/dollar exchange rate. Reflecting characteristics of the Korean economy such as its small open economy, currency and financial crises, and structural economic changes, I estimate VAR models and ECMs, treating the dollar index and oil prices as exogenous variables alongside dummy variables. The impulse response analysis reveals that during the pre-currency crisis period (April 1990-October 1997), an upward shock to (call rate-federal funds rate) caused industrial production and consumer prices to decline while increasing the won/dollar exchange rate. title: Effectuating Antitrust's Democratic Function
affiliations: Open Markets Institute

detail.title: Effectuating Antitrust's Democratic Function
detail.abstract:
The antitrust laws have a democratic function, not merely an economic one. As a fundamental legal system of political, economic, and social ordering, the antitrust laws sustain and promote the conditions necessary for democratic self-government.

This Article develops this argument through four interrelated analyses. First, this Article demonstrates that lawmakers sought to safeguard democratic institutions and promote the conditions necessary for democratic self-government when they enacted the antitrust laws, particularly the landmark Sherman Act. Second, this Article argues that Congress designed antitrust’s vast, durable, and participatory enforcement structure to function as a democratic architecture, institutionalizing oversight and remediating the harms arising from concentrated economic power. Third, this Article details how the antitrust law’s democratic architecture also incorporates a more positive dimension. It examines how federalism, the Noerr-Pennington doctrine, the labor exemption, and Parker Immunity can both restrain private domination and create and sustain the conditions for democratic ordering so that our fundamental freedoms necessary for democracy can be fully realized. Specifically, this Article focuses on Parker Immunity—the doctrine authorizing states to exempt conduct from antitrust laws—as an exemplary and underutilized mechanism for public ordering. This Article argues that Parker Immunity offers a paradigmatic example of how the antitrust laws can function both as a structural safeguard of democracy and a facilitator of it. Lastly, this Article details how antitrust’s democratic function should structure enforcement policy and provides a basic framework for evaluating whether specific conduct should be lawful under the antitrust laws.

detail.abstract: As China expands infant and toddler care services, county governments play an increasingly important role in translating national objectives into local policy arrangements. This study examines the design characteristics of county-level infant and toddler care policies and explores the contextual conditions associated with highly consistent policy designs. Drawing on policy design theory, a three-level analytical framework distinguishing substantive and procedural policy dimensions was developed and applied to 30 county-level infant and toddler care policies issued between 2020 and 2024. Policy Modeling Consistency (PMC) Index analysis was used to assess policy design, and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) was employed to identify configurations associated with high policy design consistency. The results show that most policies demonstrate acceptable to high levels of design consistency. Procedural dimensions are more fully specified than substantive dimensions, particularly regarding actor responsibilities, safeguard mechanisms, and coordination arrangements. In contrast, policy functions and evaluation provisions receive comparatively less attention. The findings also indicate that highly consistent policy designs emerge through multiple combinations of institutional, demographic, and resource conditions rather than a single developmental pathway. The study identifies a distinctive procedural–substantive structure in county-level infant and toddler care policies and highlights how local contexts shape policy design. These findings contribute to research on childcare policy and provide insights for strengthening local childcare service systems.

detail.abstract: A red card costs a World Cup team 0.66 goals over the remaining minutes of regulation. We estimate this causal effect by exploiting within-match variation in the timing of unilateral dismissals across the seven World Cup tournaments held between 1998 and 2022. A staggered difference-indifferences design applied to a match-level panel observed at five-minute intervals recovers the bin-by-bin trajectory of the response. The effect emerges shortly after the dismissal and accumulates monotonically through the remainder of the regulation. The result is robust to a standard TWFE benchmark, sample restrictions, and is sharper in group-stage than in knockout fixtures-suggesting that strategic responses to the sanction depend on tournament-design incentives. These findings provide causal evidence on the dynamic trajectory of disciplinary sanctions in elite football.

detail.abstract:
Hospital AI applications can be developed in several different ways: they can be developed by an external software development company (SDC), they can be developed internally in the hospital, or a hospital can work together with an SDC to jointly develop an AI application. The chosen arrangement has ramifications for the liability of the involved parties. The EU product liability directive, for example, hinges on considerations such as when the product is released to the market, which party qualifies as manufacturer, which level of control the manufacturer has over the released product and what constitutes a substantial modification of the product. As the directive is aimed at maximum harmonization across the EU, designating a party as manufacturer could have large effects both up and down the value chain, and on the competence of Member States to operate concurrent national regimes.  

The contribution of this paper is threefold: (i) further the conceptual understanding of the key concepts of market release, manufacturer, substantial modification, manufacturer’s control, open-source software and component/related service as regards co-creation of medical AI, (ii) study how involved parties could contractually shape these concepts, and (iii) analyse whether the rationale underlying the PLD is compatible with a value chain perspective through reviewing the impact such concepts and agreements could have on related claims along the value chain and on concurrent national regimes.

detail.title: A Model for Identifying Contractual, Fiscal and Debt-Related Risks in Infrastructure Public-Private Partnerships: Impact on Sovereign Debt and Mitigation Mechanisms
detail.abstract: Infrastructure Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) are among the most complex procurement arrangements in construction and project management, bundling design, build, finance, and operate phases into long-term contracts that create layered risk exposures extending decades beyond project delivery. While the engineering and construction management literature has extensively examined technical and operational risks, a systematic gap remains in the treatment of the contractual provisions-incomplete agreements, termination payment formulae, arbitration clauses, and guarantee structures-that translate project-level performance failures into sovereign fiscal crises. This paper develops and tests an integrated risk identification framework that connects three interdependent risk layers operating in PPP procurement: contractual risks arising from incomplete agreements and asymmetric dispute resolution mechanisms; fiscal risks generated by off-balance-sheet accounting treatment and correlated guarantee exposure; and debt-related risks linked to the enforcement architecture that compels governments to honour obligations even when economically distressed. Drawing on Jerome Roos's (2019) creditor power framework and primary source procurement documentation from Mexico, Peru, and Colombia, the paper demonstrates that legal enforcement through international arbitration, political conditionality through multilateral lender requirements, and reputational sanctions through capital market access collectively constitute an enforcement pathway that converts contingent PPP liabilities into binding sovereign debt obligations. The framework is tested empirically using the World Bank Private Participation in Infrastructure (PPI) Database 2024 and IMF World Economic Outlook data for 2,052 PPP projects across 17 Latin American and Caribbean countries over 1995-2022. Panel country fixed-effects estimation finds that a one-percentage-point increase in PPP contingent liability exposure as a share of GDP is associated with a 1.30 percentage point increase in annual sovereign debt/GDP (p = 0.097). Cox proportional hazard analysis identifies institutional quality (HR = 0.562, p < 0.001) as the primary predictor of distress timing-establishing that construction programme governance capacity, not contract terms alone, determines long-run PPP outcomes. The framework generates actionable guidance across three dimensions central to international construction management practice. First, it identifies the procurement design featurestermination payment caps, competitive tendering requirements, MDB co-financing anchors-that constitute best practice for governments procuring infrastructure PPPs. Second, it evaluates commodity-backed payment arrangements as an alternative to financial guarantees, a mechanism of growing relevance in resource-rich developing markets. Third, it identifies specific strategic implications for Chinese construction firms and state-owned enterprises navigating procurement barriers-including the SBLC guarantee incompatibility documented in Mexico's CFE procurement-and operating in high-debt sovereign risk environments. The paper concludes with a seven-pillar negotiation framework grounded in the empirical evidence and applicable to practitioners across both the public and private sides of PPP transactions.

title: Shareholder Demand for Disclosure and Firm Resistance: Evidence from 30 Years of Proposals

detail.title: Shareholder Demand for Disclosure and Firm Resistance: Evidence from 30 Years of Proposals
detail.abstract: Shareholders increasingly ask firms to disclose rather than to act. Assembling three decades of DEF 14A shareholder proposals and the SEC no-action sample of excluded proposals, I provide an anatomy of what disclosure investors demand, on what grounds, and how firms resist supplying it. The share of disclosure proposals rises from 14% to 40%, reflecting less a changing composition-toward environmental, social, and political topics and toward institutional investors-than a shift toward disclosure within those categories. The requested content ranges from factual descriptions to forward-looking and analytical assessments. The benefits and costs each side invokes map onto the channels accounting theory formalizes: proponents appeal to reductions in external and internal information asymmetry and real effects. Boards counter with direct compliance costs, indirect proprietary risks, and real effects that distort firm behavior. In 42% of disclosure proposals, boards argue that the requested information is already public, most often citing the firm's own website. These arguments predict whether the SEC permits exclusion and how shareholders vote. Compared with action proposals, disclosure proposals rest less on firm-specific circumstances or peer practices and more on regulatory mandates and expert evidence. Cross-sectional and quasi-experimental evidence further corroborates that shareholders demand disclosure over action when they disagree on policy or face uncertainty about firm fundamentals.

detail.abstract:
Corporate conflicts represent one of the most significant risks to business continuity and corporate stability. While many companies are established on the basis of personal trust among shareholders, business experience demonstrates that disputes frequently arise from diverging interests, governance failures, succession issues, and the absence of clear mechanisms for decision-making and conflict resolution.

This article examines shareholders' agreements as practical instruments for preventing corporate disputes and strengthening corporate governance. It explores their legal foundations in the principle of private autonomy, their role in regulating shareholder relations, and their growing importance in modern business structures, including startups, family businesses, and investment-driven companies.

Particular attention is given to the contribution of shareholders' agreements in preventing corporate deadlock, protecting minority shareholders, regulating share transfers, facilitating succession planning, and providing efficient dispute resolution mechanisms such as arbitration. The article also analyses the limits of contractual freedom and the various protection mechanisms available to ensure compliance with these agreements.

Drawing on legal doctrine, comparative corporate governance principles, and practical business realities, the article argues that shareholders' agreements should be viewed not merely as ancillary contracts, but as strategic governance tools capable of reducing legal uncertainty, promoting investor confidence, and enhancing business resilience. Their importance is particularly evident in emerging markets, where governance structures continue to evolve and where preventive legal mechanisms can play a decisive role in supporting sustainable business growth.

detail.abstract: Small open economies often anchor their exchange rate to a basket of foreign currencies, with weights typically set from trade shares or financial exposure. Such schemes ignore the heterogeneity of pass-through across currencies and the covariance structure of bilateral rates, and therefore do not minimize the volatility of imported inflation, the central bank’s mandate. This paper proposes a minimum-variance framework — formally analogous to a Markowitz portfolio problem in pass-through space — in which basket weights minimize the variance of exchange-rate-driven imported inflation, subject to a constraint that preserves the basket’s cumulative pass-through. Applied to the case of Fiji, an import-intensive island economy with a five-currency basket, the optimization reduces the variance of imported inflation by close to twenty percent, with results robust across alternative specifications.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether alternative measures of underlying inflation improve the historical fit of Taylor rules in prediction of actual Federal Reserve policy. Using quarterly data from 1990 to 2026 and a range of Taylor rule formulations, I show that the choice of inflation measure materially affects Taylor rule accuracy. The Trimmed Mean PCE consistently delivered a closer fit than the Core PCE, indicating that Fed policy decisions were implicitly responding to a view of underlying inflation more akin to the Trimmed Mean PCE than to the traditional Core PCE. In Q2 2026, this rule prescribes a Federal Funds Rate very close to the prevailing level, suggesting that current policy is consistent with a reaction function viewing inflation through a trimmed mean lens. Given the increasing focus in monetary policy discussions on alternative measures of underlying inflation, and the Dallas Fed Trimmed Mean PCE in particular, these findings have implications for the modeling and forecasting of Federal Reserve policy.

detail.abstract: The deployment of military personnel in response to urban crime has become increasingly salient in the United States. Yet the effectiveness and efficiency of such deployments remain largely unknown. This paper studies the effect of the August 2025 deployment of National Guard troops in Washington, DC, using administrative crime data and a tripledifferences design that compares changes before and after the August 11 deployment across treated and untreated areas, relative to analogous periods in prior years. detail.abstract: Exchange rate movements have implications for the purchasing power of residents or voters. Given that the exchange rate is often seen as a barometer of government performance, there could be strong incentives to influence exchange rate valuation during elections. This paper investigates whether political economy factors affect Foreign Exchange Intervention (FXI) policy across countries. It investigates whether central banks tend to implement FX sales, leaning against depreciations, during electoral periods in a sample of 28 countries including both advanced (AEs) and emerging (EMs) economies over the period 2000-2019. Further, this result is driven by countries where political pressures on central bank governors are more prevalent. Furthermore, the paper also finds that monetary policy transparency has the potential to mitigate this politically driven FXI during electoral period. Finally, the paper discusses policy implications given that politically motivated FX sales could hamper the ability of central banks to effectively respond to large shocks.

title: What Investors Need from Lawyers to Confront the Polycrisis: A New Prudent Investor Rule for Trust Law

detail.abstract: The interacting collection of current global risks, summarized by the term “polycrisis,” has the potential to create enormous macroeconomic damage, impoverishment, and social unrest. Unfortunately, many, if not most, societal institutions lack the incentives to confront the polycrisis because its effects are too nebulous, uncertain and long-term to mobilize collective action. In the U.S., one of the only groups that can be incentivized to mitigate the polycrisis is the class of individuals that oversee retirement accounts, because the beneficiaries of these accounts face catastrophic threats to their long-term financial security. Retirement fund trustees are fiduciaries who are obligated by law to investigate and prudently minimize material threats to their beneficiaries’ financial well-being. The material pecuniary threats of the polycrisis should be no different. In control of nearly $45 trillion, trustees of U.S. retirement accounts have the resources, awareness, and methods to mitigate the polycrisis, but are hesitant to do so. This trepidation persists even though acting to mitigate the polycrisis provides financial benefits, thus avoiding the political controversy surrounding the non-financial benefits of sustainable investing. But hesitancy might be cured by filling gaps in U.S. trust law. These gaps require urgent correction by the legal academy before the polycrisis becomes irreversible. I outline changes to the Prudent Investor Rule and suggest language to amend the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) that would allow retirement trustees to more forcefully alleviate the polycrisis. Trust law should be improved by a) returning the concept of risk to its roots in the probability of loss, turning away from its current usage as a synonym for volatility; b) introducing a duty to mitigate systemic risks on par with the duty to mitigate idiosyncratic risks; c) inserting the precautionary principle into trust law; and d) introducing a duty to educate beneficiaries about systemic risks. The paper concludes with proposed ERISA language that would codify these trust law revisions.

title: What Political Tribalism Borrows: Primary Bond Activation as the Mechanism of Durable Human Solidarity

detail.title: What Political Tribalism Borrows: Primary Bond Activation as the Mechanism of Durable Human Solidarity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes primary bond activation as the mechanism that explains why specific conditions succeed in reducing intergroup bias in the Common Ingroup Identity Model literature, while others fail. Thirty years of CIIM research has established with consistency that recategorization reduces intergroup bias under conditions of cooperative interdependence, authentic superordinate identity, prototypical messengers, and dual identity preservation. The research has not fully explained why those specific conditions succeed while their alternatives fail.

The paper proposes that the conditions that work are precisely the conditions that activate pre-political primary bonds — the social forms through which the most fundamental human capacity for solidarity is organized into community life. Political tribalism achieves its emotional power not by generating its own substrate but by recruiting the energy of primary bonds toward political competition. Because this recruitment is never complete, the bonds retain independence that can be activated by specific conditions. Those conditions are the conditions CIIM identifies as effective.

The paper develops five primary bond categories organized as a weighted web rather than a hierarchy: familial, place-based, genealogical, cowork, and scientific enterprise bonds. It identifies the three-move recruitment mechanism through which political tribalism operates on these bonds — legitimation, attribution, community — and applies the framework schematically to three communities to illustrate its analytical and predictive purchase. It then returns to the CIIM evidence base to show that the primary bond activation mechanism generates testable predictions the existing CIIM account does not make. When a recruitment operation reaches all five bond categories simultaneously — as the apparatus behind the Lost Cause mythology did across a century of institution-building — it did not feel like politics. It felt like reality. That sentence describes the mechanism’s most consequential achievement and names the target of any cross-tribal recognition strategy operating against it.

The primary bond activation mechanism has not been directly tested as proposed here. The paper offers it as an explanatory hypothesis for an existing body of evidence and as a framework for generating testable predictions. What this paper establishes on its own: the theoretical claim, the bond taxonomy, the three-move recruitment mechanism, the CIIM re-explanation, and the testable predictions that follow from the mechanism. What requires the companion papers: the full front door and back door framework with its manipulable experimental variables; the historiographical evidence base against which the mechanism’s claims can be assessed at scale; and the design principles for practitioners. The schematic community mappings in Part III illustrate the framework’s analytical purchase and are included here as orientation, not as full-depth analysis.

This paper is the first in a series. Companion papers develop the back door taxonomy and design principles for cross-tribal recognition arguments; historiographies of the Lost Cause mythology, the Protestant traditions, and the Critical Studies tradition; and a strategic design paper for practitioners. The companion papers share the theoretical framework developed here and are cited where relevant. The theoretical contribution of this paper — the primary bond activation mechanism as an explanation for the CIIM evidence base — can be evaluated independently of the companion papers. The companion papers extend the framework; they do not retroactively validate it.

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The paper develops a new monetarist DSGE model to examine the macroeconomic implications of fiat-money-backed stablecoins and the effectiveness of prudential policies in mitigating associated risks. The model features two segmented sectors: a centralized real economy where fiat money facilitates consumption and investment, and a decentralized virtual economy characterized by anonymous bilateral search and matching, in which transactions are exclusively conducted using stablecoins. Calibrated to the U.S. economy, the simulation results reveal that stablecoins amplify the propagation of exogenous shocks to key macroeconomic variables by weakening the effectiveness of monetary policy. However, prudential regulations—specifically those governing the backing ratio of stablecoins to fiat-denominated reserve assets, analogous to banking liquidity requirements—can serve as stabilizing instruments, dampening volatility and enhancing macroeconomic resilience in the presence of stablecoins.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the findings of a longitudinal survival analysis of field-level cessation of production (CoP) events in the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS) oil and gas basin, covering 477 offshore fields across 10,128 field-year observations from 1975 to 2026. The analytical method is the stratified Cox Proportional Hazards model, supplemented by Kaplan-Meier survival estimation, interrupted time series analysis, and a System Fragility Score derived from organisational ecology theory.

The primary finding is that the Energy Profits Levy (EPL), introduced in May 2022 and subsequently raised to an effective marginal rate of 78%, is the dominant fiscal predictor of field cessation. In lagged specifications, the EPL hazard ratio reaches 6.528 (p<0.001). Post-EPL observed cessation rates of 8.49% represent a deviation of 8.16 standard deviations above the pre-EPL mean of 0.41%. The interrupted time series confirms a structural break at EPL introduction: the post-EPL cessation rate multiplier is 2.64×.

The engineering predictors of cessation — water cut (HR 2.522) and decommissioning programme approval (HR 6.528) - perform as theoretically expected. The EPL finding is separable from geological depletion: water cut trends in the panel are gradual and secular, while cessation event clustering is sharp and contemporaneous with fiscal policy change. A hub contagion covariate (HR 3.104) confirms that infrastructure cascade dynamics are empirically present, providing quantitative support for qualitative concerns about Forties Pipeline System throughput. The System Fragility Score breached its self-correction threshold in 2022 and stood at 0.67 at the 2026 observation date.

The North Sea is not in geological decline. The accelerated closure rate is a fiscal phenomenon, and it is measurable.

title: Linguistic Marginalization as a Weapon of Economic Oppression: An NLP Analysis of Financial Literacy Outcomes in India
affiliations: Columbia University, Barnard College

detail.title: Linguistic Marginalization as a Weapon of Economic Oppression: An NLP Analysis of Financial Literacy Outcomes in India

declarations.funderStatement: The Laidlaw Foundation

detail.abstract: India is currently facing a "linguistic genocide" of minority languages due to the implementation of nationwide hegemonic policies. This has severe repercussions for speakers, as it contributes to cycles of intergenerational poverty. Experts suggest that many of the declining languages are spoken by Scheduled Tribes, a factor that has played a role in their widespread impoverishment. To build on these claims, this study employed AI-based corpus analysis and statistical modeling to investigate the relationship between the availability of financial literacy terms and financial literacy outcomes across different language groups. Additional factors such as language vitality, script type, geographic region, and population density were also assessed to evaluate their influence. The results revealed a significant correlation between the presence of financial literacy terms and financial literacy outcomes, with language vitality and script type serving as key explanatory variables. Languages with the lowest percentages of financial literacy terms and financial literacy scores typically belonged to historically marginalized tribal groups. These findings underscore the role of linguistic exclusion in perpetuating poverty and highlight the urgent need for financial literacy education in local languages. In response, this paper identifies systemic barriers to equitable financial literacy education for marginalized tribal communities and advocates for reform.

title: Imagination and the Philosophy of Belonging: Ontological Openness, Creativity, and Human Transformation

detail.title: Imagination and the Philosophy of Belonging: Ontological Openness, Creativity, and Human Transformation
detail.abstract:
This article develops a comprehensive theory of imagination within the Philosophy of Belonging. It argues that imagination is not merely a secondary cognitive faculty, a form of escapism, or an aesthetic supplement to rationality, but a fundamental ontological mechanism rooted in the imperfect structure of existence itself. Because reality is relational, open, and non-ergodic, human beings confront a world characterized by uncertainty, entropy, conflict, and irreversible historical transformation. Under such conditions, imagination becomes indispensable for survival, meaning creation, scientific discovery, artistic expression, religious experience, and institutional innovation.

The article situates imagination within the broader framework of the Philosophy of Belonging, including imperfect belonging, stratified reality, and dual temporality. It argues that imagination performs several interconnected functions: it enables human beings to project “sufficient harmonies” in the absence of certainty; it deepens existential belonging through art, symbols, rituals, and narratives; it constitutes the psychological infrastructure upon which reason and scientific modeling depend; and it makes creativity, freedom, and civilizational transformation possible.

Rather than opposing imagination to reason, the article demonstrates that rationality itself emerges from deeper emotional, relational, and imaginative structures. Scientific theories, political systems, economic institutions, and religions are interpreted as historically evolving imaginative constructions through which humanity attempts to organize reality and expand forms of belonging. Imagination therefore becomes the bridge between synchronic structures and diachronic transformation, between present limitations and unrealized possibilities. The human capacity to imagine reflects the unfinished and open character of existence itself

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: More frequent large macroeconomic shocks since the global financial crisis have entrenched uncertainty, particularly in Europe. This has increased the premium on central bank communication in guiding expectations and strengthening macroeconomic resilience. European central banks have responded by adapting their communication toolkits and styles. This study provides a systematic assessment of recent central bank communication across advanced and emerging European economies, combining a survey of institutional communication frameworks with novel text-miningbased indicators on monetary policy guidance in these economies over 2009-2025. While communication toolkits are broadly similar, their intensity and transparency differ markedly, with central banks in advanced economies making greater use of forward-looking tools. Central banks in both groups respond primarily to inflation uncertainty. However, communication strategies diverge, as central banks in advanced economies increasingly shift toward forward-looking language, whereas those in emerging markets shift toward more backward-looking communication. These patterns highlight credibility and institutional capacity as key determinants of central bank communication under uncertainty.

detail.abstract: This paper studies probabilistic forecast combination in low-sample elimination tournaments. These settings are challenging because outcomes are sparse, the champion is a rare event, and knockout paths are endogenously selected. Using the FIFA World Cup as an application, I examine whether a transparent structural forecast and market-implied probabilities contain complementary information when evaluated by proper scoring rules. The structural component is a family of Poisson count models that map pre-tournament information into team strengths, including FIFA ranking, tradition, host and confederation indicators, reconstructed Elo ratings, recent competitive form, and defending-champion status. I also evaluate regularized match-level Poisson models and score-weighted structural pools. The market component converts bookmaker odds into normalized implied probabilities. Forecasts are combined through a convex linear pool, with weights chosen by leave-one-tournament-out validation. In 115 group-stage matches from the 2014, 2018, and 2022 World Cups with historical 1X2 odds, the best combined forecast reduces average log loss from 0.9660 for the selected structural model and 0.9750 for the market benchmark to 0.9466. The multiclass Brier score falls from 0.5700 and 0.5644 to 0.5544. The selected system is then applied to the expanded 2026 World Cup using 100,000 Monte Carlo paths.

title: Introduction To Gravity Model for Beginners

detail.title: Introduction To Gravity Model for Beginners
detail.abstract: This paper provides a didactic, beginner-friendly review of the gravitational model and its conceptual translation from classical physics into international economics. After a brief introduction, it begins by establishing the structural and mathematical parallels between Newton's law of universal gravitation and the economic gravity equation, demonstrating how economic mass (GDP) attracts commercial flows while geographic distance acts as spatial resistance. The paper then examines the deterministic philosophical framework necessary to apply rigid natural laws to collective human behavior. Finally, it traces the chronological evolution of the literature, mapping the historical divergence between the physics-rooted approach of early demographers and Walter Isard, and some of the utility-based econometric adaptations. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that despite globalization, spatial friction remains a vital, measurable force in shaping global commerce and geopolitical interactions.

This paper examines the evolving intersection between competition law and the "marketplace of ideas," contrasting the legal frameworks and recent developments in the United States and Spain. Historically, antitrust regulation aimed to preserve a diverse influx of information to protect democratic discourse, a principle deeply rooted in U.S. overseeing the very media outlets that monitor its actions. Ultimately, the paper underscores the ongoing consolidation within traditional media and argues that as media mergers increasingly impact both freedom of enterprise and democratic expression, Spanish antitrust authorities may inevitably face a resurgence of claims grounded in the defense of political and informational pluralism.
Through a comparative lens, the study analyzes recent shifts in U.S. antitrust enforcement—highlighted by regulatory interventions in ideologically motivated cases such as Children’s Health Defense v. WP Company LLC and State of Texas v. BlackRock, Inc.—which demonstrate a renewed willingness to regulate non-price viewpoint competition when it yields adverse economic repercussions. Conversely, the Spanish legal system historically decoupled ideological disputes from antitrust scrutiny, delegating the evaluation of media pluralism during mergers to sector-specific governmental bodies rather than independent competition authorities. This institutional design faces criticism due to the executive branch's inherent conflict of interest in overseeing the very media outlets that monitor its actions. A Repair Framework for Portfolio Optimization after Markowitz
